lessons.title: Read the README's words
lessons.originalTitle: The words in the README, before lesson 0
lessons.summary: The first read for newcomers: what a compiler pipeline is, what LLVM IR and a pass are, how opt loads a plugin, what a CFG and control-flow flattening mean, and what verify does and does not prove.
lessons.takeaway: Know what a pass is before you write one.

blocks.text: This section exists because the README (and the lessons that follow) assume you already know what a "pass", "IR", and "CFG" are. It is not part of the numbered lessons; read it once, then start at lesson 1.
What is a compiler, and where does LLVM fit?

A compiler translates a program you wrote in a language like C++ into machine instructions a CPU executes. Modern compilers are built in stages, and each stage reads one representation of the program, inspects or improves it, and hands a new representation to the next stage:

C++ source  ->  [front end]  ->  LLVM IR  ->  [mid-end: passes]  ->  LLVM IR'
            ->  [back end]  ->  machine code  ->  object file  ->  executable

**Clang** is the front end: it turns `.c`/`.cpp` files into LLVM IR. **LLVM** is the rest of the pipeline's infrastructure: the intermediate representation itself, plus libraries of analyses (things that inspect the IR and report facts about it) and transformations (things that rewrite it), and the tools to load and run them.
MiniShield does not compile C++ programs. It is a plugin loaded into `opt`, LLVM's command-line IR tool (below), which then runs MiniShield's passes over `.ll` IR files.
What is LLVM IR?

LLVM IR (intermediate representation) describes a program in terms of typed values and instructions, before any specific CPU is chosen. A minimal example (this is the entire `minishield-input.ll` fixture):

items: `@add_one` is a **function**; `i32` is a 32-bit integer type; `%x` is a typed value.

`entry:` names a **basic block**: a straight-line run of instructions with a single entry point and no jumps inside it. A block always ends with a **terminator** instruction that transfers control (`ret`, `br`, ...).

`%result = add i32 %x, 1` is one **instruction**; the name `%result` is defined exactly once and only used after that definition. This "define once, use later" property is called **SSA** (static single assignment).
The files in `tests/ir/` (for example `tests/ir/phi.ll`) are handwritten text IR, one small function each.

blocks.text: What is a pass?

A **pass** is one program-level inspection or transformation that LLVM runs over the IR. A pass receives an object (here: a `Function`), inspects or changes it, and returns a result describing what it did. Think of a pass as a function that LLVM calls for you, once per function, in the order you scheduled.

MiniShield has two so far: `StatsPass` only counts instructions and prints a report (a read-only pass), and `FlatteningPass`, which will restructure the function's control flow (a transformation pass, not yet implemented).
What is `opt`, and what is a pass plugin?
`opt` is LLVM's command-line tool for IR: it reads an IR file, runs a **pipeline** of passes, and writes IR back (or just prints diagnostics). Out of the box, `opt` only knows LLVM's built-in passes.

A **pass plugin** is a small shared library (here `build/libMiniShield.so`) that `opt` loads at start-up when you pass `-load-pass-plugin=...`. The loading happens through the system's `dlopen()` mechanism: the library is read into memory and its exported entry point `llvmGetPassPluginInfo` is called. That entry point hands back the pass names the plugin provides (`minishield-stats`, `minishield-flatten`), so after loading, `-passes='function(minishield-stats)'` can name your pass. The plugin is therefore a load-time relationship with `opt`, not a link-time one (lesson 2 explains why that decides the CMake library type).
The comma in `-passes='function(minishield-stats),verify'` is the pipeline: run the named function pass on every function, then run the built-in `verify` pass over the module.
What are control flow, a CFG, and control-flow flattening?

**Control flow** is the order in which a program's instructions execute, determined by its branches. An `if` statement means "these instructions, or those, depending on a condition", and a `while` loop means "these instructions, possibly again".
The **control-flow graph (CFG)** makes that order explicit: basic blocks are nodes, and every possible "go to next block" transfer is an edge. The function in `tests/ir/phi.ll` has four blocks:

entry -> left  -> join
       \       /
        right ->   (join ends the function with ret)
`entry` has two successors (its conditional branch can choose either), `join` has none (it ends in `ret`).

**Control-flow flattening** is a transformation that takes a structured CFG like that and rewires it into a shallower, harder-to-follow shape: many small basic blocks, all at the same level, joined by a dispatcher — usually a loop plus a big `switch` over block identifiers that decides which block runs next. The program still computes the same results, but the visible control flow becomes one long sequential loop instead of the original if/else or loop structure. Flattening is used in binary hardening and obfuscation (attackers' tools find it harder to reconstruct the original logic), which is why MiniShield's goal is a safe flattener: it must accept only functions whose flow it fully understands and leave everything else byte-for-byte untouched.

**Natural loops** (mentioned in the README and lesson 17) are the loops a specific standard algorithm finds: take a **back edge** (an edge from a block to an earlier block that dominates it — dominates meaning every path from the entry to that block passes through it) and collect every block that can reach the loop header without going through the exit. LLVM's `LoopAnalysis` computes exactly these; in `tests/ir/loop.ll` the edge `body -> header` is the single back edge, and the natural loop is `{header, body}`.
What do "function eligibility" and "diagnostic stub" mean?

**Eligibility** is the yes/no decision made before a flattening pass rewrites a function: is this function's shape one the pass can handle? The current policy (lesson 23) rejects, among other things, functions with exception handling, coroutine intrinsics, block addresses used as values, or terminators the pass does not model (only `br`, `switch`, `ret`, `unreachable` are accepted). An accepted function is **eligible**; a rejected one must be left completely unchanged — lesson 25 shows how to prove that with a diff. Eligibility is a conservative "we can handle this shape" decision, not a proof that flattening is safe in general.

A **stub** is a placeholder implementation: the interface exists and runs, but the real work is not there yet. At the start of this project, `FlatteningPass::run` only prints the function name and block count; it changes nothing. The word **diagnostic** (as in "diagnostic stub") says the stub's job is to report observations, not to transform. By lesson 23 the stub also prints the eligibility decision.
What are conda, CMake, and Ninja, in one line each?

items: **Conda** (here via **Miniforge**, a conda distribution that defaults to the conda-forge channel) is a package and environment manager. The `minishield` environment is a self-contained directory with its own compiler, LLVM 23.1.5, build tools, and libraries, so the project does not depend on what the host machine happens to have installed. "Activating" it puts that environment's tools at the front of the shell's command search path.
**CMake** is the configure step: it reads `CMakeLists.txt`, locates the installed LLVM, and generates build instructions. It does not compile anything itself.
**Ninja** is the build step: it executes the generated instructions (`build/build.ninja`), compiling only the changed files and linking the plugin.

blocks.text: The four-step chain — create the environment, activate it, configure with CMake, build with Ninja — is exactly the lesson 1 checkpoint.
What do the `opt` flags in the README mean?

opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-stats),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-output.ll

items: `-load-pass-plugin=...` loads MiniShield's `.so` so its pass names exist.
`-passes=...` is the pipeline to run; `function(X)` means "run X once per function in the module".
`verify` is a built-in pass that checks the IR's structural rules.
`-S` prints the result as text IR; without it, `opt` writes compact binary IR by default.
`-o file` writes the transformed IR to a file; `-disable-output` keeps the IR in memory and writes nothing — used when you only want the diagnostics the pass printed.

blocks.text: What is a fixture?

A **fixture** is a small, stable input file kept in the repository (here the `.ll` files under `tests/ir/`) whose expected results are known by hand. You run your tool on the fixture and compare the output to the expectation (the table in lesson 12). "Fixture" comes from test setup being fixed in place: nobody edits a fixture to make a test pass.
Valid vs. correct: what `verify` does and does not prove

`verify` checks that the IR obeys LLVM's structural rules: types agree, every value is defined exactly once before use (SSA), every PHI node has an incoming value from each predecessor block, return types match the function's type, and so on. IR that passes is **valid** (well-formed).

**Correctness** — does the transformed program compute the same results, with the same side effects, as the input — is a separate, stronger property. `verify` does not check it: a pass can emit perfectly valid IR that behaves differently. That is why lesson 14's empty-diff check (the pass must leave the IR unchanged while it is a stub) and, later, real testing, are the actual safety nets.
Study-session walkthrough — separate the program being compiled from the pass doing the work

Separate the compiler-side plugin from the program described by LLVM IR. First identify which tools build the plugin, which tool loads it, and which later tools produce an executable. This orientation makes the following API exercises easier to place.
Before writing, answer: When I run opt, am I executing the C function, compiling the C++ pass, or transforming the LLVM program?

your C++ pass sources → compiler/linker → libMiniShield.so
LLVM input module + opt + that plugin → inspected or rewritten LLVM module
LLVM module + backend + caller → an executable program

There are two programs to keep separate: the compiler-side plugin and the program described by its input IR. Printing a message in StatsPass executes inside opt; creating an LLVM add inserts a computation for the target program to execute later. A successful plugin build does not by itself run either a test input or the target function.
Task: Small writing step: Point to one file belonging to the plugin and one file describing an input program. Identify the command responsible for each arrow.

Checkpoint: Explain what opt -disable-output suppresses: it prevents writing the transformed module, not compiler-side diagnostic printing. Before writing a pass, be able to name which program each code example belongs to.

items: `-disable-output` suppresses the output module: `opt` keeps the IR in memory and writes nothing — no `-o` file, no printed IR. It does not suppress compiler-side diagnostic printing: the pass's `llvm::errs()` reports still reach stderr, which is exactly why the flag is used when you only want the diagnostics the pass printed.

There are two programs to keep separate. The compiler-side plugin — your C++ pass sources (`lib/Plugin.cpp`, `lib/FlatteningPass.cpp`) that the compiler/linker turn into `build/libMiniShield.so` — is the code that runs *inside* `opt`. The target program — the LLVM IR module (for example `tests/ir/phi.ll` or `tests/ir/minishield-input.ll`) — is the program `opt` inspects or rewrites. So printing a message in `StatsPass` executes inside `opt`, while creating an `add` instruction inserts a computation for the target program to execute later; a successful plugin build does not by itself run either one.

lessons.title: Create your environment
lessons.originalTitle: Create the minishield Conda environment
lessons.summary: Start with a consistent toolchain. Understand what Conda installs, what activation changes, and why the compiler needs development headers.
lessons.takeaway: Environment first, project second.

blocks.text: Volume 1 builds toward one decision — which functions a control-flow-flattening pass may touch. Everything before that decision is inspection, and inspection needs a plugin that actually loads. This part is the ground every later lesson stands on: a consistent Conda toolchain and a CMake project that turns your source into a loadable library.
Goal: give the project one consistent Linux C++ toolchain, LLVM release, build system, and test library.
The recorded environment was originally created with this command (confirmed in its conda-meta/history):
conda create -y -n minishield -c conda-forge clang lld llvmdev gtest cmake ninja

Conda downloaded prebuilt packages and their dependencies. It did not compile LLVM from source. That unpinned command resolved LLVM/Clang 23.1.5 in this study session; running it later can select a different release.
Create the study environment reproducibly
For a fresh setup on Linux x86-64, first install Conda or Miniforge and initialize its Bash integration if necessary. Then, from this repository:

conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate minishield

The environment name comes from name: minishield in environment.yml. Creating the environment installs packages into a separate prefix; activating it changes the current shell's PATH and sets CONDA_PREFIX so commands resolve to this toolchain. Activation does not compile this project.
If Conda is installed but activation is unavailable in Bash, load the shell hook from your own installation. In the recorded machine it was:

source "$HOME/miniforge3/etc/profile.d/conda.sh"
conda activate minishield

The setup file pins clang, lld, and llvmdev to 23.1.5 to keep the plugin's headers and runtime compatible. It is a study environment specification, not a byte-for-byte lockfile of every dependency. Package availability and platform still matter.
Know what each dependency does

rows: C/C++ compiler for the plugin and future input programs
LLVM headers, library development files, and CMake package metadata
LLVM linker available for toolchain work
GoogleTest for the later C++ test suite
Configures the project and generates Ninja build instructions
Executes the generated compile and link rules
Standard C++ headers such as type_traits, matching this session's runtime

blocks.text: The initial environment had the C++ runtime but lacked its development headers. During the build lesson we added libstdcxx-devel_linux-64 16.2.0. The repository specification includes it from the start. A missing type_traits error concerns C++ standard-library headers, not the path to LLVM headers.
For an existing environment missing those headers, the normal package-install command is:
conda install -n minishield -c conda-forge libstdcxx-devel_linux-64=16.2.0
Verify the environment before building

conda activate minishield
clang --version
clang++-23 --version
opt --version
llvm-config --version
cmake --version
ninja --version
The LLVM tools should report the same 23.1.5 release. This environment exposes clang++-23 rather than a plain clang++; pin that compiler in CMake instead of falling back to the host compiler.
Before linking in this environment:
export LIBRARY_PATH="$CONDA_PREFIX/lib"

LIBRARY_PATH supplies link-time library search paths used by the compiler driver. It is different from LLVM_DIR, which tells CMake where to find LLVMConfig.cmake, and from LD_LIBRARY_PATH, which affects runtime library loading.
Checkpoint: distinguish these four operations: install the environment, activate the environment, configure the project with CMake, and build the project with Ninja. They are separate steps.

items: Install the environment: `conda env create -f environment.yml` (the recorded session used `conda create -y -n minishield -c conda-forge clang lld llvmdev gtest cmake ninja`) downloads prebuilt packages into a separate prefix. It compiles nothing and changes no shell.

Activate the environment: `conda activate minishield` changes only the current shell — it puts the environment's `bin/` at the front of `PATH` and sets `CONDA_PREFIX`, so commands resolve to the environment's tools (the LLVM 23.1.5 release, including `clang++-23` rather than a plain `clang++`). Activation does not compile the project, and a new terminal starts unactivated.

Configure with CMake: `cmake -G Ninja -S . -B build ...` reads `CMakeLists.txt`, locates the installed LLVM through `-DLLVM_DIR` / `find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)`, and *generates* `build/build.ninja`. It does not compile anything itself.
Build with Ninja: `cmake --build build` executes the generated instructions, compiling only the changed files and linking `build/libMiniShield.so`.

blocks.text: Study-session walkthrough — activation selects tools; the manifest describes their installation

Treat environment.yml as the package recipe and activation as a change to the current shell’s tool selection. If minishield already exists, inspect its tools before recreating anything. A working environment and a configured project build are separate prerequisites.
Before writing, answer: What changes when I activate minishield, and why can a new terminal accidentally use different tools?

conda activate minishield
command -v opt
opt --version
llvm-config --version

environment.yml records the named environment and its dependencies. Creating it installs packages; activation selects their paths for the current shell. Headers and libraries are development inputs, while executables such as opt and clang are tools you run. The project directory and its build directory are separate from the environment. LLVM headers, the compiler, and opt must belong to the compatible release used by the plugin.

Task: Small writing step: Inspect the existing environment and tool versions first. Read the manifest entries before changing any package; do not create a second environment merely to repeat a successful setup.

Checkpoint: Check that the selected opt/llvm-config report the intended LLVM 23 toolchain. When linking with this Conda setup, also set LIBRARY_PATH as the setup section explains; activation and compiler library search are distinct pieces of the configuration.

items: After `conda activate minishield`, check what the shell actually selected: `command -v opt` should point inside `$CONDA_PREFIX/bin`, and `opt --version` and `llvm-config --version` should both report the intended 23.1.5 release. A fresh terminal can silently fall back to different (host) tools, which is why you verify the selected tools instead of assuming the activation worked.

Before linking, `export LIBRARY_PATH="$CONDA_PREFIX/lib"` adds that directory to the conda clang driver's *link-time* `-L` search, because its default search paths (the gcc-layout directories and the sysroot) do not include where the `libstdcxx` package installed `libstdc++.so`; without it the link fails with `x86_64-conda-linux-gnu-ld: cannot find -lstdc++`. Activation (which `PATH` entries the shell uses) and `LIBRARY_PATH` (which directories the driver searches at link time) are distinct pieces of configuration, and `LIBRARY_PATH` is different from `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (runtime library loading) and from `LLVM_DIR` (where CMake finds `LLVMConfig.cmake`).

quiz.q: Which step creates build.ninja?
choices: Activating the Conda environment
Running CMake’s configure/generate command
Running opt on a fixture
quiz.why: Conda supplies tools. CMake reads CMakeLists.txt and generates Ninja’s build instructions.

lessons.title: Define your CMakeLists
lessons.originalTitle: Understand what CMake is configuring
lessons.summary: Read the project's CMakeLists line by line against a three-line hello-world baseline: what the target is, how LLVM is found, and why a plugin differs from a program.
lessons.takeaway: Every CMake line answers a question a hello-world project never has to ask.

blocks.text: Task: read CMakeLists.txt and identify the target named MiniShield.

add_library(MiniShield MODULE ...) describes a loadable plugin. The listed .cpp files are compiled and linked into build/libMiniShield.so. The MODULE library is loaded by opt at runtime through -load-pass-plugin.
A hello-world CMakeLists to start from
The smallest CMakeLists.txt that does anything useful is three lines:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.15)
project(HelloWorld CXX)
add_executable(hello main.cpp)

items: `cmake_minimum_required` sets a version floor: CMake refuses to run if it is older than this.
`project(HelloWorld CXX)` names the project and enables the C++ compiler.
`add_executable` defines one target: a program. CMake compiles `main.cpp` and links `build/hello`.

blocks.text: With that file, `cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build` works and you run `./build/hello`. Notice what is not there: no package discovery, no compiler flags, no include paths, no link libraries, no output location. Every one of those omissions is possible because hello-world has no dependencies and produces a program that you run directly.

MiniShield's CMakeLists.txt has none of that by accident: every extra line exists because the project consumes a prebuilt third-party library and produces a plugin that `opt` loads, not a program you run.
MiniShield's CMakeLists, line by line
The project's file makes four moves.
**Move 1 — pick the language and standard (lines 1–6).**

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.15)
project(MiniShield CXX)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)

Same opening as hello-world, plus decisions hello-world can skip: LLVM 23's headers require C++20, so the standard is pinned (`REQUIRED ON` makes a downgrade an error, not a warning), and `CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS` writes `build/compile_commands.json` so clangd and IDEs can index the project.
**Move 2 — find LLVM (lines 10–12).**

set(LLVM_LINK_LLVM_DYLIB ON)
find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)
message(STATUS "Found llvm ${LLVM_PACKAGE_VERSION} at ${LLVM_DIR}")

Hello-world needs no packages; this project needs the prebuilt LLVM the Conda environment installed. `find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)` locates the `LLVMConfig.cmake` that the configure step's `-DLLVM_DIR` points at; that file defines `LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS`, `LLVM_DEFINITIONS`, and the imported `LLVM` target this file uses in the next moves. `REQUIRED` makes a missing LLVM a hard configure error instead of a later, mysterious failure.
**Move 3 — define the target (lines 16–19).**

add_library(MiniShield MODULE
    lib/Plugin.cpp
    lib/FlatteningPass.cpp)

This is the hello-world divergence in one keyword. Hello-world says `add_executable`: build a program with a `main()`. MiniShield says `add_library ... MODULE`: build a loadable shared library with no `main()`. Nothing links against MiniShield; `opt` `dlopen()`s it at run time. (`STATIC` would be an archive no one can `dlopen`; `SHARED` would declare a "you may link me" relationship that does not exist — see the `add_library` deep dive below.)
**Move 4 — attach the requirements (lines 21–32).**

separate_arguments(MS_LLVM_DEFS NATIVE_COMMAND ${LLVM_DEFINITIONS})
target_compile_definitions(MiniShield PRIVATE ${MS_LLVM_DEFS})
target_include_directories(MiniShield PRIVATE
    ${LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS}
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)
target_link_libraries(MiniShield PRIVATE LLVM)
set_target_properties(MiniShield PROPERTIES LIBRARY_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR})

Hello-world compiles against the standard library and needs none of this.
The plugin has five requirements, all target-scoped and all `PRIVATE`
because nothing links against MiniShield. Each command answers one
question; they configure the target, and compilation and linking happen
later, when the build runs.

**`separate_arguments` — turn a flag string into a list.** CMake has no
array type: a "list" is a `;`-separated string. `LLVMConfig.cmake` stores
`LLVM_DEFINITIONS` as *one* space-joined string (e.g.
`"-D_GNU_SOURCE -D_GLIBCXX_USE_CXX11_ABI=1 -D__STDC_FORMAT_MACROS"`), so
passed as-is it would reach the compiler as a *single* argument — one giant
macro name containing spaces and `=`, which the compiler rejects.
`separate_arguments(MS_LLVM_DEFS NATIVE_COMMAND ${LLVM_DEFINITIONS})`
splits it into individual `-D` flags (`NATIVE_COMMAND` applies the current
platform's quoting rules). You need this only when a variable is a
space-joined string rather than a list; variables you create yourself
(`set(X a b c)`) are already lists.

**`target_compile_definitions` — preprocessor definitions for this
target.** Attaches the split `-D` flags to MiniShield's compile line only.
The classic LLVM-consumer snippet uses the directory-global
`add_definitions(...)`, which would leak LLVM's flags into every target
added later; the target-scoped form keeps them on the one target that needs
them (see the deep dive on target scope below).

**`target_include_directories` — where to find headers.** Adds LLVM's
header directories and this project's `include/` to the compiler's search
paths (typically as `-I` options), so source files can include LLVM and
project headers. Including a header does not link LLVM's implementation: a
declaration is not code, so this line alone leaves the target unable to
resolve LLVM's symbols.

**`target_link_libraries` — which libraries to link.** `LLVM` is the
imported target supplied by `find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)`; CMake
uses its metadata to locate the existing `libLLVM-23.so` and construct the
link command. This is the line that supplies the implementation the
headers declared — and because it is the same library `opt` already loads,
the process ends with one LLVM, not two. The project does not build LLVM;
it only consumes the installed shared library.

**`set_target_properties` — named settings on the target.**
`LIBRARY_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}` chooses where the built
module is written: with `cmake -S . -B build` and Ninja, that is
`build/libMiniShield.so`, the path the README's `opt` commands point at.
It changes the destination, not the filename or the link dependencies
(a multi-configuration generator may append a subdirectory such as
`Debug/`).
**Side by side.**

rows: an executable — a program you run
a MODULE shared library — a plugin opt loads
none — a plugin is entered by opt, not by the OS
C++20, forced — LLVM 23 headers require it

blocks.text: Every difference traces back to one sentence: hello-world produces a program you run, with no dependencies, while MiniShield produces a plugin opt loads that must match opt's exact LLVM release. The three-line file works because it has no decisions to make; the 35-line file is mostly the record of decisions it does.
Checkpoint: explain why finding a header and linking a library are separate operations. Including a declaration does not supply compiled implementation.

items: Headers are declarations, not code: `target_include_directories(MiniShield PRIVATE ${LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS} ...)` only adds LLVM's header directories (as `-I` options) to the compiler's search paths, so source files can name LLVM types and functions and be type-checked. Including a header does not link LLVM's implementation — a declaration is not code, so this line alone leaves the target unable to resolve LLVM's symbols.

Linking is the separate operation that supplies the implementation: `target_link_libraries(MiniShield PRIVATE LLVM)` resolves the imported `LLVM` target (declared by `find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)`) to the prebuilt `libLLVM-23.so`, and its machine code satisfies the symbol references the compiler emitted. The two lines answer different questions — where are the declarations, versus where is the compiled library code — and because it links the same library `opt` already loads, the process ends with one LLVM, not two.

blocks.title: Why `find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)`?

blocks.text: `find_package(<name>)` can locate a package in two different ways, and the `CONFIG` keyword selects which:

rows: A CMake community contributor, shipped **inside CMake itself**
The **LLVM package author**, shipped *with the package* (e.g. `$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/cmake/llvm/` for the conda-forge `llvmdev` package)
A hand-maintained script that probes paths and compilers

Declares the exact truth about *this build*: imported targets (the `LLVM` dylib target), variables (`LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS`, `LLVM_DEFINITIONS`, `LLVM_PACKAGE_VERSION`), and helpers (`llvm_map_components_to_llvmlib`)
Nothing to find — CMake ships ~162 `Find*.cmake` modules and **no** `FindLLVM.cmake`
Works: the config file is installed with the LLVM package

blocks.text: So `find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)` means: *"the package name is `LLVM`; don't look for a CMake-contributed finder script — find the configuration file that the installed LLVM package ships."*
**How the search resolves** (config mode), in priority order:

items: `LLVM_DIR` — a variable named after the package + `_DIR`. This build passes `-DLLVM_DIR=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/cmake/llvm`, which is the top-priority hint and removes all ambiguity.
`CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH` (if set).
System prefixes (`/usr/local`, `/usr`, …), probing subpaths such as `<prefix>/lib/cmake/llvm` and `<prefix>/share/cmake/llvm`.

blocks.text: **The three "package" layers** — the same word does three jobs here:

conda package   "llvmdev"          → the distribution unit on disk (what was installed)
CMake package   "LLVM"             → the logical contract: "I want to consume LLVM"
config file     "LLVMConfig.cmake" → the file that fulfills the contract (what CONFIG selects)
`find_package(LLVM ...)` names the **CMake** package; `CONFIG` selects the **file** that answers for it; the conda package is just the delivery mechanism that installed that file.

**Rule of thumb:** if the vendor ships a `FooConfig.cmake`, use `find_package(Foo CONFIG)`. Find-modules are for ancient libraries that predate config files. Config files are maintained by the people who *built* the library, so they're accurate for that exact build (correct C++ standard, component list, dylib imported targets); community Find-modules are often years behind, and for LLVM they don't exist at all.

blocks.title: Do the two search modes affect artifact size or rebuild time?

blocks.text: **No — the search mode is a pure discovery mechanism.** `find_package` is a *finder*, not a *builder*: it runs once at configure time and only fills in variables and imported targets (`LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS`, `LLVM_DEFINITIONS`, the `LLVM` imported target, …). Whichever mode supplies those, the same downstream decisions are made by the same `add_llvm_library` / `target_link_libraries` calls:

find_package (module mode) ─┐
                            ├─► same variables / imported targets ─► same flags ─► same link line ─► identical .so
find_package (config mode)  ┘

If a `FindLLVM.cmake` existed and pointed at the *same* installation that `LLVMConfig.cmake` points at, the result would be byte-identical: same include dirs, same definitions, same `libLLVM-23.so` on the link line — no recompilation, no size change. The mode only becomes visible if the two routes disagree about *which* LLVM they find; then the difference comes from different installations, not from the mode.
The three axes, kept separate:

rows: **Which installation** is found (e.g. conda 23.1.5 vs anything else)
Yes — different headers/ABI → our sources recompile
**Yes** — tens of KB vs hundreds of MB

blocks.text: So: **mode = discovery, installation = compatibility, link strategy = size.** `CONFIG` buys nothing in bytes or build time — it buys *correctness and determinism* (the package author's own truth about their build, and for LLVM the only route that exists at all).

blocks.title: Where does the size go? (`MODULE` + dylib linking)

blocks.text: Measured in this environment (conda-forge LLVM 23.1.5):

items: `libLLVM.so.23.1` (the shared library): **188 MB** — prebuilt, already loaded by `opt`
the static component archives (`libLLVMCore.a`, `libLLVMPasses.a`, …): **363 MB total**

blocks.text: The small-plugin outcome comes from the **`MODULE` + dylib-linking** combination, not from the `find_package` mode:

items: **This project:** `MiniShield` is built as a `MODULE` (a `dlopen()`-able `.so` containing *only* our ~5 `.cpp` files — tens of KB). With `LLVM_LINK_LLVM_DYLIB ON`, every LLVM symbol resolves **at load time** from the *same* `libLLVM-23.so` that `opt` uses — one LLVM in the process.

**Static alternative** (linking the component archives): those symbols are copied into our `.so` → it bloats toward hundreds of MB, *and* you get duplicate-LLVM-in-one-process corruption (two sets of globals), *and* every relink re-copies that pile. Bigger and wrong, not smaller and safer.
**`SHARED` vs `MODULE`:** on Linux they produce nearly identical `.so` files — the difference is contractual, not mechanical. Details in the next section.

blocks.text: Recompilation story: editing MiniShield code → recompile 5 files, relink a small `.so` (seconds). Switching LLVM releases → recompile our files against the new headers. We never compile LLVM itself (hours/days) — consuming the prebuilt 188 MB shared library is the point. You can't hot-swap the LLVM `.so` under a running `opt`, so versions must match: **one release only.**

blocks.title: What does `add_library` do?

blocks.text: `add_library(<name> [STATIC | SHARED | MODULE] [EXCLUDE_FROM_ALL] <srcs>…)` creates a **library target**: a named node in CMake's build graph carrying sources, compile/link rules, and the *usage requirements* attached by the `target_*` commands (below). The type keyword sets the artifact and its contract (Linux):

rows: code is *copied into* each consumer at its link time
yes — every consumer embeds its own copy (how you get "two LLVMs in one process")
*linked against* at build time; consumers record a `DT_NEEDED` entry
*loaded at runtime* via `dlopen()` — a plugin, not a dependency
**no** — CMake refuses to link a MODULE into another target

blocks.text: **Why `MODULE` for MiniShield:** the relationship between `opt` and the plugin is `dlopen()` at runtime — a load-time, not link-time, relationship. Nothing ever *links against* MiniShield, so `STATIC` is out (an archive is not a loadable image) and `SHARED`, while mechanically near-identical on Linux, would declare a "you may link me" relationship that doesn't exist. `MODULE` declares the plugin contract — which is also why all link scopes are `PRIVATE`.
Mechanically, for a real target (`add_library(MiniShield MODULE lib/Plugin.cpp lib/FlatteningPass.cpp)`):

items: one **compile rule per source** → `build/CMakeFiles/MiniShield.dir/…o`, compiled with the target's standard, definitions, and include dirs;
one **archive/link rule** → the artifact, by default named `libMiniShield.so` (default `lib` prefix) at the build root — pinned explicitly by `LIBRARY_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR}`;
the **target node** itself, which `ninja -C build` builds and the `target_*` commands attach properties to.

blocks.text: **The same command has a second role — describing things you do *not* build.** `LLVMConfig.cmake` line 1775 contains:
add_library(LLVM SHARED IMPORTED)

An *imported* target builds nothing; it is pure metadata describing an existing binary (`libLLVM-23.so`: location, soname, link interface). `target_link_libraries(MiniShield PRIVATE LLVM)` links against that description, resolved to the real `.so` at link time. One command, two directions:

add_library(MiniShield MODULE …)   producer:  "build this artifact from these sources"
add_library(LLVM SHARED IMPORTED)  consumer:  "here is an existing .so, its properties are…"

(`add_llvm_library` — unavailable here, see below — was simply LLVM's in-tree wrapper around `add_library` with extra LLVM build plumbing; plain `add_library` is the correct consumer-side replacement.)

blocks.title: Why target-scoped `target_*` instead of `add_definitions` / `include_directories`?

blocks.text: You'll find the classic LLVM-consumer snippet in older docs and tutorials:

separate_arguments(LLVM_DEFINITIONS_LIST NATIVE_COMMAND ${LLVM_DEFINITIONS})
add_definitions(${LLVM_DEFINITIONS_LIST})
include_directories(${LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS})

It *works*, but both `add_definitions(...)` and `include_directories(...)` are **directory-global**: they apply to *every* target defined in that directory (and subdirectories, until overridden) — your pass, and every test or tool you add later. The modern style is **target-scoped**, i.e. each target declares its own requirements:

separate_arguments(MS_LLVM_DEFS NATIVE_COMMAND ${LLVM_DEFINITIONS})
target_compile_definitions(MiniShield PRIVATE ${MS_LLVM_DEFS})
target_include_directories(MiniShield PRIVATE
    ${LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS}
    ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)
Why prefer target scope:

items: **No leakage.** Flags and include paths attach to the target that actually needs them; future targets (Day-3 test binaries, benchmark harnesses) start from a clean slate instead of inheriting LLVM's definitions by accident.

**Explicit dependency graph.** A target's requirements are readable on the target itself, which is exactly what CMake's *usage requirements* model (`PRIVATE` / `PUBLIC` / `INTERFACE`) is built around.

blocks.text: The scope keywords, for reference:
`MiniShield` is a `MODULE` (a `dlopen()`-able `.so` that nothing links to), so everything is `PRIVATE`.
Two more details from that snippet worth keeping:

items: `separate_arguments(... NATIVE_COMMAND ...)` does **real work** here: `LLVMConfig.cmake` sets `LLVM_DEFINITIONS` as a single *space-joined string* (e.g. `"-D_GNU_SOURCE -D__STDC_FORMAT_MACROS ..."`), not a CMake list, so it must be split into individual `-D` flags before use. The `NATIVE_COMMAND` mode selects the current platform's command-line quoting rules; on Linux it uses Unix-style parsing.

The tutorial's `add_subdirectory(<pass name>)` is a *layout* choice (one subdirectory per pass/chapter), not a linking mechanism. This project uses a single top-level `CMakeLists.txt` and adds exactly one subdirectory later: `tests/`, for the standard CTest/GoogleTest setup.

blocks.text: Study-session walkthrough — give headers, linked symbols, and output paths different jobs

Use target_include_directories, target_link_libraries, and set_target_properties for different jobs: finding declarations, resolving compiled library code, and selecting output properties. Attach each setting to the target it affects rather than treating all three as ways to locate LLVM.
Before writing, answer: Why is finding an LLVM header not enough to produce a loadable plugin?

target_include_directories(MiniShield PRIVATE ${LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS})
target_link_libraries(MiniShield PRIVATE LLVM)
set_target_properties(MiniShield PROPERTIES
    LIBRARY_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR})

This CMake fragment belongs after target creation. Include paths help the C++ compiler find declarations while compiling source files. Linking resolves the LLVM functions/types’ out-of-line code through the imported LLVM library. The output-directory property chooses where the built module is placed; it does not find headers or register a pass. PRIVATE limits these usage requirements to this target in this initial module-only layout.

Task: Small writing step: Explain each line against the error it could address: missing header, unresolved library symbol, or looking for the .so in the wrong directory. Keep the reusable-core changes for Volume 3 separate.

Checkpoint: Reconfigure after changing CMake and rebuild. Finding LLVMConfig.cmake discovers package information; it does not magically compile missing project .cpp files or teach opt a pipeline name.

items: Reconfigure (`cmake -G Ninja -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER="$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/clang++-23" -DLLVM_DIR="$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/cmake/llvm"`) should complete with CMake reporting that configuration and generation succeeded — it prints `Found llvm 23.1.5 at ...`, and the `Could NOT find ZLIB / LibXml2 / zstd` warnings are harmless — and then `cmake --build build` recompiles the changed files and relinks `build/libMiniShield.so`.

That result proves only the discovery step: finding `LLVMConfig.cmake` fills in `LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS`, `LLVM_DEFINITIONS`, and the imported `LLVM` target. It does not compile project `.cpp` files you forgot to list in `add_library` (the source list decides what is compiled and linked into the plugin), and it does not teach `opt` any pipeline name (that comes from the parsing callback in `Plugin.cpp`). The real check comes after: an `opt` run with `-load-pass-plugin` and the named pass must recognize the name and run.

quiz.q: What does target_include_directories provide?
choices: Compiled LLVM implementation
The runtime loader’s library path
Header search paths for compilation
quiz.why: Includes let the compiler find declarations. Linking supplies the compiled implementation.

lessons.title: Configure, then compile
lessons.originalTitle: Generate the build instructions before trying to build
lessons.summary: Generate build.ninja before asking Ninja to execute it. Learn to distinguish a configuration failure from a compilation error.
lessons.takeaway: Configure → generate → compile → link.

blocks.text: Task: from the project root, activate the environment and configure CMake:

conda activate minishield
export LIBRARY_PATH="$CONDA_PREFIX/lib"

cmake -G Ninja -S . -B build \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER="$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/clang++-23" \
  -DLLVM_DIR="$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/cmake/llvm"

The `export` line in the task is not a CMake option — it is the environment the compiler runs in. When Ninja links the plugin, conda's clang driver searches for libraries only in its default `-L` paths (the gcc-layout directories and the sysroot), and those do not include `$CONDA_PREFIX/lib`, where the environment's `libstdcxx` package installed `libstdc++.so` — the C++ standard library the plugin links against. `LIBRARY_PATH` adds that directory to the driver's link-time search. Without it, configuration and compilation succeed and the link step fails with `x86_64-conda-linux-gnu-ld: cannot find -lstdc++`. Note what it is not: not `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (runtime library loading) and not `LLVM_DIR` (which tells CMake where to find `LLVMConfig.cmake`).
The options mean:

-G Ninja: use Ninja as the generated build system.
-S .: read the source project's CMakeLists.txt here.
-B build: place generated files in build/.
CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE: select Release settings.
CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER: use this environment's C++ compiler.
LLVM_DIR: locate this LLVM installation's CMake configuration.
Wait for CMake to report that configuration and generation succeeded. Then:
cmake --build build
This second command runs the generated build instructions. It does not replace the initial configure/generate step.

Observed error: Ninja could not find build.ninja. The build directory had CMakeCache.txt, but generation had not completed. Running the configuration command successfully created build.ninja. A cache file alone is insufficient.
Observed result: "ninja: no work to do" means the target is up to date. It is not a test result or an indication that the plugin failed.

Environment issue encountered: the compiler could not find <type_traits>. The Conda environment had the runtime but lacked its matching C++ development headers. Installing libstdcxx-devel_linux-64 16.2.0 supplied those headers. The LIBRARY_PATH export addresses the separate linker search for libstdc++.

blocks.title: Known environment quirks (conda-forge LLVM 23.1.5)

blocks.text: Verified against this environment; each of these bit the actual build:

items: **No `LLVM.cmake` / `AddLLVM.cmake` in the installed package.** `include(LLVM)` finds nothing useful and `add_llvm_library` / `llvm_map_components_to_llvmlib` are unavailable — they are part of LLVM's *in-tree* build infrastructure, not the installed package's CMake API. `LLVMConfig.cmake` does the dylib wiring itself (`set(LLVM_LINK_LLVM_DYLIB yes)` and `add_library(LLVM SHARED IMPORTED)` → `libLLVM-23.so`), so the correct consumer pattern is plain CMake: `add_library(MiniShield MODULE ...)` + `target_link_libraries(MiniShield PRIVATE LLVM)`.

**No plain `clang++` in the env** — only `clang` and `clang++-23`. Pin the compiler explicitly: `-DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/clang++-23` (`$(which clang++)` is empty and silently falls back to the system g++).

**`LIBRARY_PATH` is required for conda's clang at link time.** `export LIBRARY_PATH=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib` — the driver's `-L` search paths are the gcc-layout dirs and the sysroot, and do *not* include `$PREFIX/lib` where the `libstdcxx` package installed `libstdc++.so`; without it the link fails with `x86_64-conda-linux-gnu-ld: cannot find -lstdc++`.

**Cosmetic warnings are expected.** `LLVMConfig.cmake` probes optional dependencies and prints `Could NOT find ZLIB / LibXml2 / zstd`. They're harmless for a pass plugin: those libraries are already inside the shared `libLLVM-23.so`.

blocks.text: Study-session walkthrough — build.ninja comes from configuration, not from the build command

If cmake --build build reports “loading build.ninja: No such file or directory,” check whether configuration and generation completed first. Ninja cannot execute build instructions that CMake has not successfully generated; this is different from a later C++ compilation failure.
Before writing, answer: Which command creates the build instructions, and which command executes them?

cmake -G Ninja -S . -B build \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER="$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/clang++-23" \
  -DLLVM_DIR="$CONDA_PREFIX/lib/cmake/llvm"
cmake --build build

Run from the project root with the environment active. -S selects source configuration and -B selects generated build state. -G chooses Ninja. The configure step reads CMakeLists and generates build.ninja only when it completes successfully. --build then invokes the configured build tool. A C++ compilation error occurs later and has a different remedy.
Task: Small writing step: Run configuration first and resolve its first real failure before attempting the build. Do not create an empty build.ninja by hand.

Checkpoint: The later “ninja: no work to do” message means the build graph considers its outputs up to date; it is not a test result. Run an opt smoke/verification command next rather than interpreting an unchanged build as proof of correct behavior.

items: `ninja: no work to do` means the build graph considers its outputs up to date — no source file is newer than the `build/libMiniShield.so` the earlier build produced. It is not a test result, nor an indication that the plugin succeeded or failed; it simply means there was nothing left to compile or link.

So the next step is a behavioral check, not another build: run an `opt` smoke/verification command, for example `opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' -S tests/ir/minishield-input.ll -o build/minishield-output.ll`. You expect the plugin to load, the stub to print `[MiniShield] function: add_one, blocks: 1`, and `verify` to pass. Only that run shows the pass actually executes; an unchanged build shows only that nothing needed rebuilding.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between the CMake step and the build step?
choices: The build command re-runs configure, so only speed differs
Configure generates build.ninja; the build command then executes those instructions
The build command generates build.ninja and does not need configure
quiz.why: Configure/generate produces build.ninja from CMakeLists.txt. The second command runs the generated instructions; it does not replace configure.

lessons.title: Give each file a job
lessons.originalTitle: Split the plugin into an entry point and a pass
lessons.summary: Separate the plugin entry point, the pass declaration, and the pass implementation. Follow the path from a header to a shared library.
lessons.takeaway: A declaration and a definition solve different problems.

blocks.text: Now the toolchain is in place; this part makes LLVM actually run your code. You split the plugin into an entry point, a pass declaration, and a pass implementation, then prove the result loads by having opt find your pass. Every later pass — stats, analysis, and flattening — runs only if this chain works, so each link is built and checked on its own.
Task: create the pass interface, its implementation, and its registration:
Recall: what a pass is, and how a plugin supplies one

A pass is one program-level inspection or transformation that LLVM runs over the IR: it receives an object (here, a `Function`), inspects or changes it, and returns a result describing what it did (Background). The plugin's job is to make `opt` call it. With `-load-pass-plugin=...`, `opt` loads the shared library through `dlopen()` and calls its exported `extern "C"` entry point `llvmGetPassPluginInfo()`, which returns a `PassPluginLibraryInfo`. One of the callbacks that structure registers with LLVM's `PassBuilder` — `registerPipelineParsingCallback` — is where the pipeline name `minishield-flatten` becomes `FPM.addPass(FlatteningPass())`; lesson 6 traces that registration.

A pass's `run()` receives `llvm::Function &F` and `llvm::FunctionAnalysisManager &AM`, and returns `llvm::PreservedAnalyses`: the set of analyses still valid after the pass ran. `PreservedAnalyses::all()` says nothing was invalidated — correct for a read-only or stub pass like this one — while `PreservedAnalyses::none()` says recompute everything.

An analysis is a registered class whose `run()` computes and returns data instead of modifying the IR. A pass asks for that data with `AM.getResult<CFGAnalyzer>(F)`; the manager computes it once and caches it, and the same `PreservedAnalyses` bookkeeping keeps the cache honest. The `CFGAnalyzer` declaration comes in lesson 16.

include/minishield/FlatteningPass.h — class and run() declaration
lib/FlatteningPass.cpp             — run() definition
lib/Plugin.cpp                     — plugin entry point and registration

Each file has one job. The header is the interface: it declares the class, and because each .cpp file is compiled on its own, Plugin.cpp must include it to see the declaration. CMake must list lib/FlatteningPass.cpp as well: the source list decides what is compiled and linked into the plugin.
For a function pass, run() receives:

llvm::Function &F
llvm::FunctionAnalysisManager &AM
It returns llvm::PreservedAnalyses. The initial implementation only reports the function name and block count, so it returns PreservedAnalyses::all().

Observed mistakes: the header was initially named FlatteningPass.cpp, while the includes requested FlatteningPass.h. Rename the declaration file to .h. Plugin.cpp also needed semicolons after the callback registration expression and the returned aggregate initializer. Read the compiler location and check the surrounding statement boundaries when diagnosing these syntax errors.
Study-session walkthrough — a header declaration, implementation, and plugin entry point are not interchangeable

Give the pass declaration, its method definitions, and plugin registration separate files. If an include requests FlatteningPass.h while the declaration was saved under a .cpp name, fix the filename/include agreement. Also check complete C++ statements and aggregate initializers when the compiler reports missing semicolons.
Before writing, answer: Why does listing an implementation in CMake not replace including its class declaration?

FlatteningPass.h   declares the pass class and its run() interface
FlatteningPass.cpp defines that class’s run() behavior
Plugin.cpp         exposes the plugin entry point and registers parsing callbacks

This is a file-role sketch. Each .cpp is compiled as a translation unit; it must see the declarations it uses through includes. The linker later combines compiled definitions. The plugin entry point returns LLVM’s version/name/registration information, while run() implements the per-function operation. Giving a declaration file the wrong name breaks the include contract before pass behavior is involved.

Task: Small writing step: Write/check the header interface first, include it from both users, then supply exactly one matching method definition. Read compiler diagnostics around complete C++ statements and aggregate initializers.

Checkpoint: A successful link establishes that referenced definitions were supplied. Loading the module and recognizing a pipeline name are subsequent checks. Keep those layers separate when locating the next error.

items: A successful link establishes one thing and only one: every symbol the plugin referenced was supplied — `lib/Plugin.cpp` and `lib/FlatteningPass.cpp` compiled, and the definitions (for example `FlatteningPass::run` and the aggregate returned from `llvmGetPassPluginInfo`) resolved into `build/libMiniShield.so`.

Loading the module and recognizing a pipeline name are subsequent, separate checks: loading is `opt` `dlopen()`-ing the `.so` through `-load-pass-plugin` and calling the exported `llvmGetPassPluginInfo()` entry point; recognition is the `registerPipelineParsingCallback` callback matching `minishield-flatten` and calling `FPM.addPass(minishield::FlatteningPass())`.

Keep those layers separate when locating the next error: a link error (an unresolved definition) points at the C++ sources or the CMake source list; a load failure points at the `.so` path or the plugin's exported entry point; an unknown-function-pass error points at the registration callback or the spelling in the `-passes` string. A green link proves none of the later layers, so it must not make you skip them.

quiz.q: Why does Plugin.cpp include the pass header?
choices: Because the header compiles the implementation into every file
Because each .cpp compiles on its own and the header is where the class is declared
Because including the header links the implementation into the plugin
quiz.why: The header is the interface: it declares the class. Because each .cpp compiles separately, including it makes the declaration visible. Linking, not the include, supplies the implementation.

lessons.title: Optional or required?
lessons.originalTitle: Choose optional or required pass behavior explicitly
lessons.summary: Choose deliberately whether LLVM may skip your pass. The installed LLVM 23 headers are the source of truth.
lessons.takeaway: Required affects skipping; it does not schedule a pass.

blocks.text: Task: compare PassInfoMixin, OptionalPassInfoMixin, and RequiredPassInfoMixin in the installed llvm/IR/PassManager.h.

PassInfoMixin supplies shared metadata such as the pass name and pipeline printing. In this installation it retains optional behavior for compatibility. The header recommends inheriting from an explicit optional or required mixin.

OptionalPassInfoMixin<T>: isRequired() is false; the pass may be skipped.
RequiredPassInfoMixin<T>: isRequired() is true; normal pass-skipping
                          mechanisms must not skip the scheduled pass.

For example, an optional function pass may be skipped on an optnone function. A required pass still runs there. Required does not automatically schedule the pass: pipeline registration and invocation are still necessary.
We used OptionalPassInfoMixin for the flattening stub. We chose RequiredPassInfoMixin for statistics because inspection should also report functions marked optnone.

blocks.title: `PassInfoMixin` vs `OptionalPassInfoMixin` vs `RequiredPassInfoMixin`

blocks.text: The New Pass Manager uses mixins to supply pass metadata, such as the pass name and pipeline printing. In this project's installed LLVM 23.1.5 headers, the relationship is:

rows: Common metadata base; still supports the older spelling with optional behavior
Explicitly declares a pass that may be skipped
Explicitly declares a pass that normal pass-skipping mechanisms must not skip

blocks.text: Both explicit mixins inherit from `PassInfoMixin<T>`. The installed header recommends that actual passes inherit from `OptionalPassInfoMixin` or `RequiredPassInfoMixin`, rather than directly from the common base.

For example, an optional function pass may be skipped on a function marked `optnone`; a required pass still runs there. **Required does not automatically add the pass to a pipeline:** it must still be registered and scheduled. See LLVM's [required-pass documentation](https://llvm.org/docs/WritingAnLLVMNewPMPass.html#required-passes).
For the initial diagnostic stub, declare the choice explicitly:

If MiniShield must perform hardening even on `optnone` functions, use `RequiredPassInfoMixin<FlatteningPass>` instead. This choice controls whether the pass may be skipped; it does not change which functions the flattening algorithm can safely handle or which analyses remain valid after `run()`.
Study-session walkthrough — required changes skipping behavior, not scheduling

Choose optional or required pass behavior deliberately. The mixin answers whether LLVM may skip the pass on inputs such as optnone functions; it does not load the plugin, register a pipeline name, or schedule the pass automatically.
Before writing, answer: If StatsPass is required, why must I still give opt the minishield-stats pipeline name?

This is an interface fragment. The CRTP-style base receives the derived class type and supplies pass information/policy. In this LLVM installation plain PassInfoMixin retains optional behavior for compatibility; explicit optional/required bases state the intended policy more clearly. We chose a required statistics pass so diagnostic inspection can run even on optnone input; flattening remained optional.
Task: Small writing step: Choose and explain the mixin for each pass. Leave parser registration and pipeline invocation as explicit separate work.

Checkpoint: Use an optnone fixture to check skipping behavior once registration works. Do not treat “required” as meaning the pass is always present in every compiler pipeline, automatically loaded, or semantically necessary for the target program to run.

items: Once registration works, exercise the skipping policy on the `optnone` fixture: run `minishield-stats` over `tests/ir/instruction-kinds.ll` — its `without_optimization` function carries `optnone`, and because `StatsPass` inherits `RequiredPassInfoMixin` (`isRequired()` is true) the pass still runs there and must produce its report. Run the optional `minishield-flatten` on the same input: declared with `OptionalPassInfoMixin`, it may be skipped on that `optnone` function, so one fixture demonstrates both behaviors.

`required` is only a skipping policy, not a presence guarantee: it decides whether normal pass-skipping mechanisms may skip the pass, but it does not load the plugin (that is `-load-pass-plugin`), register the pipeline name (that is the parsing callback), or schedule the pass automatically — required does not automatically add the pass to a pipeline; it must still be registered and scheduled. It is also unrelated to the target program: the pass is an inspection tool `opt` runs, and nothing about the program's own behavior requires it.

quiz.q: What does RequiredPassInfoMixin guarantee?
choices: The pass is automatically added to every pipeline
Normal optional-pass skipping does not skip a scheduled pass
The pass preserves all analyses
quiz.why: Required affects whether a scheduled pass may be skipped. Registration, scheduling, and preservation are separate decisions.

lessons.title: Teach opt your pass name
lessons.originalTitle: Register the pass name that opt will recognize
lessons.summary: Register a parsing callback that turns a pipeline name into a pass instance. A class alone is not a runnable pipeline.
lessons.takeaway: Recognize the name. Add the pass. Return true.

blocks.text: Task: understand llvmGetPassPluginInfo() in Plugin.cpp.
The exported entry point returns PassPluginLibraryInfo containing the LLVM plugin API version, the plugin name, the plugin version, and a callback that registers passes with PassBuilder.

Use llvm/Plugins/PassPlugin.h in this installed LLVM version. Return the header-provided LLVM_PLUGIN_API_VERSION; no custom plugin-version macro is needed. The plugin's own version string is distinct from that API version.
The installed function-pipeline parsing callback takes:

llvm::StringRef Name
llvm::FunctionPassManager &FPM
llvm::ArrayRef<llvm::PassBuilder::PipelineElement> InnerPipeline

It recognizes a name, adds the corresponding pass to FPM, and returns true. It returns false for a name it does not handle. Our simple passes also reject unexpected nested pipelines by checking InnerPipeline.
Checkpoint: trace how the string minishield-flatten results in constructing FlatteningPass and adding it to the function pass manager.

items: Before any parsing happens, `opt` loads `build/libMiniShield.so` through `-load-pass-plugin` (`dlopen`) and calls the exported `llvmGetPassPluginInfo()`. The returned `PassPluginLibraryInfo` includes the callback that calls `PB.registerPipelineParsingCallback(...)`, which installs the function-pipeline parsing callback with the `PassBuilder`.

When the pipeline parser reaches the element inside `function(minishield-flatten)`, it hands the name `minishield-flatten` to the registered callback, together with the `FunctionPassManager` (`FPM`) and the inner pipeline (empty for a simple name).

The callback first rejects an unexpected nested pipeline (`if (!InnerPipeline.empty()) return false;`), then compares `Name == "minishield-flatten"`. On a match it executes `FPM.addPass(minishield::FlatteningPass())` — constructing the pass object and scheduling it in the function pass manager — and returns `true`; any other name returns `false`, and the parser reports the element as unknown.

When the pipeline later runs, the function pass manager invokes `FlatteningPass::run(F, AM)` once per function — that is where the string becomes behavior: the string names nothing by itself, and only the callback's `addPass` turns it into a concrete pass instance.

Registration connects a pipeline string to a C++ pass object. The parser asks whether the plugin understands a requested name, and the callback schedules the corresponding object. Defining a class alone does not teach opt its user-facing name.
Before writing, answer: Where does the string minishield-stats become a call to StatsPass::run?

This is a parsing-callback fragment, not a standalone function. Name is the string being parsed. FPM is the function pass manager that owns the scheduled pass instance. Returning true means this callback recognized the requested element; it is a C++ parser result, not a boolean computed by the target program. The callback must also have the correct installed LLVM signature.
Task: Small writing step: Add one recognized name and ensure its declaration is included in Plugin.cpp. Rebuild the .so before loading it.

Checkpoint: A typo in the command string, an unregistered name, or a stale plugin can all look like an unknown-pass failure. Loading the shared library successfully proves only that loading worked, not that this callback recognized the requested pipeline element.

items: The three causes converge on the same symptom — an unknown-function-pass error: a typo in the `-passes` string means the name never matches the callback's comparison; an unregistered name means the class exists but the callback has no branch that adds it (defining a class alone does not register it); a stale plugin means the `cmake --build build` after the registration edit failed, leaving the previous `.so` on disk, which `opt` loads without complaint but whose callback lacks the new branch.

A successful load proves only the load-time relationship: that `dlopen` found the `.so` and its exported `llvmGetPassPluginInfo` ran. Recognition of the pipeline element is a separate, later step inside the parsing callback, and load success tells you nothing about it. So on an unknown-pass failure, check the layers in order: the command string's spelling, the callback's branch (including that `Plugin.cpp` includes the pass header), and that the plugin was actually rebuilt after the registration change.

lessons.takeaway: Valid IR is not a proof of equivalent behavior.

blocks.text: Task: use the repository fixture tests/ir/minishield-input.ll:
Run from the project root with the Conda environment activated:

opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/minishield-input.ll \
  -o build/minishield-output.ll
Expected diagnostic from the stub:
[MiniShield] function: add_one, blocks: 1

The pipeline runs the flattening pass on functions, then verifies the module. -S selects text IR; -o chooses the output file. For diagnostics alone, use -disable-output instead of requesting an output IR file.

verify checks LLVM IR structural rules: types, SSA constraints, PHI incoming edges, return types, and related invariants. It normally succeeds silently. It does not prove that transformed code has the same behavior as the input.
Observed error: function(minishield-flatten)] had an extra closing bracket. Pipeline syntax must be valid before LLVM can run any pass.
Study-session walkthrough — a balanced pipeline is checked before the pass runs

Check pipeline syntax before investigating pass behavior. An expression ending in function(minishield-flatten)] has a mismatched closing bracket and cannot be parsed as the intended pipeline. Correct that spelling before expecting the pass to inspect a function.
Before writing, answer: What does verify establish, and why did a stray ] stop the command before any transformation?

opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/minishield-input.ll -o build/smoke-checked.ll

The shell quotes keep the pipeline as one argument. function(...) wraps a function-pass pipeline; the following comma schedules module verification. -S requests textual IR, and -o names generated output. verify checks IR rules such as typing, terminators, and dominance; it does not prove that the rewritten program returns the original answers.
Task: Small writing step: Correct only the unmatched bracket/parenthesis first, then rerun the smoke command after a successful build.

Checkpoint: Distinguish pipeline-parse failure, plugin-load failure, verifier failure, and wrong program results. A well-formed unchanged stub can pass verify, and a well-formed wrong transformation can too. The before/after example and later behavioral tests answer different questions.

items: Pipeline-parse failure: the `-passes` string is not valid pipeline syntax — the observed error was an extra closing bracket in `function(minishield-flatten)]`. `opt` rejects it before running any pass, because pipeline syntax must be valid before LLVM can run anything.

Plugin-load failure: `opt` cannot load the `.so` named by `-load-pass-plugin` (missing file, wrong path, or an incompatible plugin export). This fails at load time, before the pipeline is even parsed.

Verifier failure: `verify`, the built-in pass that checks structural rules (types, SSA constraints, PHI incoming edges, return types), rejects IR that the pipeline produced — the pass emitted structurally invalid IR.
Wrong program results: the IR passes `verify` yet behaves differently from the input — a well-formed wrong transformation.

The last two are indistinguishable to `verify`, which is the point of the checkpoint: an unchanged stub and a wrong-but-valid rewrite both pass it, so validity says nothing about behavior. The before/after example answers “did this pass change anything?” (for a read-only pass the IR must stay unchanged), while later behavioral tests answer “does the transformed program still compute the same results?” — different questions, different evidence.

lessons.title: Declare the statistics pass
lessons.originalTitle: Start task 1.2 by declaring StatsPass
lessons.summary: Build a small function-pass interface before implementing traversal. Keep declaration and definition in agreement.
lessons.takeaway: Start with the smallest useful interface.

blocks.text: With a plugin that loads, you can write your first pass end to end: a read-only stats pass that walks each function's blocks and instructions and counts what it finds. Counting is the safe way to learn the traversal, because it changes nothing — you are reading IR, not rewriting it. The same loop shapes up for the analysis that follows.
Task: write `include/minishield/StatsPass.h`, using the `FlatteningPass.h` header from lesson 6 as the model.

The statistics pass is a read-only **function pass**. Its header is an interface, not the traversal: it names the class, chooses the mixin, and declares the `run()` signature. The implementation comes later in `lib/StatsPass.cpp`. Start from this template, which leaves the pass declaration to fill in:
Step 1 — Add the header guard and the pass infrastructure

#pragma once
#include "llvm/IR/PassManager.h"
`#pragma once` tells the compiler to include the file at most once. `llvm/IR/PassManager.h` supplies the types the pass references: `Function`, `FunctionAnalysisManager`, and `PreservedAnalyses`.
Step 2 — Name the pass and choose its mixin
class StatsPass : public llvm::RequiredPassInfoMixin<StatsPass> {

The class is named `StatsPass` and lives in `namespace minishield`. It inherits publicly from `llvm::RequiredPassInfoMixin<StatsPass>`, a mixin named for the class itself. `Required` tells the pass manager this pass must run when it is scheduled (lesson 6); `OptionalPassInfoMixin` would let it be skipped, which a statistics pass does not want.
Step 3 — Declare the `run()` method

`run()` takes the function it inspects (`F`) and the function analysis manager (`AM`), and returns `llvm::PreservedAnalyses` describing which cached analyses stay valid. A function pass inspects one function at a time; the pass manager supplies the function and calls `run()` on it. The method is declared here and defined later in `lib/StatsPass.cpp`.
The full implementation
Checkpoint: compare the declaration with the later definition. Class name, namespace, parameter types, and return type must agree.

items: The header declares the interface: class `StatsPass` in `namespace minishield`, publicly inheriting `RequiredPassInfoMixin<StatsPass>`, with the public method `llvm::PreservedAnalyses run(llvm::Function &F, llvm::FunctionAnalysisManager &AM);`. It says `run` borrows a mutable `Function` and an analysis manager and returns preservation information — a promise made to both `Plugin.cpp` and `StatsPass.cpp`.

The out-of-line definition in `lib/StatsPass.cpp` must agree with it on all four axes: the namespace (`minishield`), the class name (`StatsPass`), the parameter types (`Function &` and `FunctionAnalysisManager &`, in that order), and the return type (`PreservedAnalyses`). The compiler matches the definition to the declaration exactly on these, which is why the lesson says to check the declaration against the intended definition before adding counting logic — any deviation (a value instead of a reference parameter, a missing `minishield::` qualifier, a different return type) is a compile error.

blocks.text: Study-session walkthrough — finish a small interface before solving its behavior

Start StatsPass with a small header interface, then supply its implementation and registration separately. Completing a class declaration does not provide the method definition or add a name to the loaded plugin.
Before writing, answer: Which promise does the header make to Plugin.cpp and StatsPass.cpp?

This public declaration belongs in the pass class. It says run borrows a mutable Function and an analysis manager and returns preservation information. It does not allocate a new function, define a traversal, or execute automatically. The out-of-line definition must agree in namespace, class name, parameter types, and return type. LLVM supplies the function when its manager runs the pass.
Task: Small writing step: Check the declaration against the intended definition before adding counting logic. Include the header in the implementation and plugin source.

Checkpoint: A header can compile in one file while another translation unit still lacks its include. The next integration lesson handles the namespace-member error and unknown pipeline name separately; neither should be “fixed” by duplicating the class definition in Plugin.cpp.

items: Each `.cpp` is compiled as its own translation unit and sees only the declarations it includes: `StatsPass.cpp` can compile fine with `#include "minishield/StatsPass.h"` while `Plugin.cpp` — which forgot that include (or included `FlatteningPass.h` twice instead) — fails with “no member named 'StatsPass' in namespace 'minishield'”. The CMake source list supplies the implementation at link time; it does not replace includes at compile time.

The two integration errors are separate, and each has its own fix: the namespace-member error is a compile-time visibility problem (add the include in `Plugin.cpp`), and the unknown pipeline name is a registration problem (extend the parsing callback to `FPM.addPass(minishield::StatsPass())` and rebuild the `.so`). Duplicating the class definition in `Plugin.cpp` would fix neither: it breaks the single-definition rule (the same class defined in two translation units), and the callback would still have no name registered — so neither error should be “fixed” that way.

quiz.q: Why does StatsPass inherit RequiredPassInfoMixin<StatsPass>?
choices: To let the pass register its own pipeline name
To preserve all cached analyses automatically
To tell the pass manager this pass must run when it is scheduled
quiz.why: Required says the pass must run when scheduled; it does not schedule the pass or preserve analyses. The mixin is named after the class it modifies.

lessons.title: Walk blocks and instructions
lessons.originalTitle: Count blocks and instructions before classifying instructions
lessons.summary: Count instructions in a nested traversal. Learn where the function pass manager stops and your iteration begins.
lessons.takeaway: Four blocks. Five instructions. Count them by hand.

blocks.text: Task: write `lib/StatsPass.cpp`. Include the `StatsPass` header, `Function.h`, and `raw_ostream.h`. Define `run()` inside `namespace minishield`.

The function pass manager already visits functions and hands each one to `run()`. Your job is the traversal inside. Start from this template, which declares the definition and leaves the body to fill in:
Step 1 — Skip declarations

if (F.isDeclaration())
    return llvm::PreservedAnalyses::all();
A declaration has no function body to inspect, so return before traversing. `PreservedAnalyses::all()` records that nothing changed; there is nothing to invalidate.
Step 2 — Count the instructions in a nested traversal
Iterate each `BasicBlock` and, inside it, each `Instruction`. `F.size()` supplies the block count. The `const` references make the read-only intent visible — the pass inspects, it does not mutate.
Step 3 — Report and return
Print to `llvm::errs()` (stderr) so the report does not mix with IR printed to stdout. No IR changed, so preserve all analyses.
The full implementation
Checkpoint using phi.ll: merge has four blocks and five instructions: three branches, one PHI, and one return.

items: Run the stats pass on `tests/ir/phi.ll` and check the report for function `merge`: four blocks (`entry`, `left`, `right`, `join` — `F.size()` supplies the block count) and five static instructions in total: three branch instructions (the conditional `br i1 %condition, label %left, label %right` in `entry`, plus the unconditional `br label %join` in each of `left` and `right`), one PHI (`%value = phi i32 [ 10, %left ], [ 20, %right ]` in `join`), and one return (`ret i32 %value` in `join`).

That count is what a hand count gives you: read labels for blocks and actual instruction lines for instructions — the `; preds = ...` text is a printer comment, not an instruction. The report is only correct if the traversal visits every block and every instruction exactly once (the nested `for (const llvm::BasicBlock &BB : F)` / `for (const llvm::Instruction &I : BB)` loop), so a wrong total points at the traversal before you add any classification.

blocks.text: Study-session walkthrough — the function manager already chose the function

Count blocks and instructions before classifying opcodes. A small initial traversal gives you an independent checkpoint: if the total is wrong, investigate traversal before adding more counters that depend on it.
Before writing, answer: Do I need another module-to-function loop inside a function pass, and does the range-for loop copy the LLVM objects?

This fragment belongs inside run(). F is already the function selected by LLVM’s function pass manager. Each reference names an existing block or instruction without copying it. A const view is sufficient for counting because inspection should not mutate IR. Reset counters for each run() invocation so one function’s result does not accumulate into the next.
Task: Small writing step: First report only the block total and instruction total. Hand-count phi.ll before adding any classification branch or switch.

Checkpoint: The fixture has four blocks and five instructions. Count static instructions, not runtime visits: a loop can execute one static instruction many times. Printing diagnostics and incrementing C++ counters should leave canonical LLVM output unchanged.

items: Counting is static, not dynamic: the counters count what is written in the IR, so one static instruction may execute many times at runtime (in a loop, the body's `add` runs once per iteration but counts once). That is why the counts are properties of the fixture, predictable by hand, and independent of any input.

The traversal must not touch the program: `StatsPass` only prints to `llvm::errs()` (stderr) and increments C++ counters in host memory — it inserts, deletes, or rewrites no instruction, and returns `PreservedAnalyses::all()` because no IR changed. So the canonical LLVM output is identical with and without the pass, and the diagnostic lines never mix into the IR stream.
