rows: `define` starts a function body. `@merge` is the module-level function name; `i32` immediately before it is the return type. Parentheses contain typed inputs supplied by the caller; braces contain its blocks.

i1 means one bit: 0 is false and 1 is true for a condition; i32 means a 32-bit integer bit pattern; signed interpretation comes from operations such as slt or sdiv, not from a separate signed i32 type.

The left side names the result of this instruction. Each SSA result has one static defining instruction; input arguments are values supplied at function entry. A name is a handle for a value, not a mutable source variable or a guaranteed CPU register.

The colon defines a block label; the label operand names a jump destination. `%` is also used for local result/argument names, so use the type/context to distinguish a value from a block target. `@` instead identifies a module-level symbol.

Everything after a semicolon on that line is a comment for the reader. The printer lists incoming blocks after preds; it is not an instruction, an execution order, or a separate edge definition. Branch/switch operands actually define the edges.

blocks.text: Every instruction used in this pair

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. `br i1 %C, label %A, label %B` goes to A for true and B for false; their order matters. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Define one value by the edge just used to enter this block. Each `[ VALUE, %PREDECESSOR ]` pairs an incoming value with its source block; it is not an array access. The PHI’s i32 type applies to every incoming value, so a literal inside a bracket does not repeat the type. PHIs go at the start of a block. On a loop’s first entry choose its entry value, and on a back edge choose its carried value. Multiple PHIs select incoming values together, rather than sequentially overwriting each other.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

Call merge with condition = true: take left and obtain 10; with false, take right and obtain 20. In a PHI listing join chooses the incoming constant using the predecessor edge. In a demoted listing only the executed path stores its constant, and join reads that value.

minishield-flatten -> add FlatteningPass

anything else     -> return false
Step 1 — Add the source to the CMake target

add_library(MiniShield MODULE

Step 2 — Include the header and register the name

A source list supplies the implementation at link time; it does not replace an include. Add `#include "minishield/StatsPass.h"` to `Plugin.cpp`, then add a branch to the parsing callback so `minishield-stats` constructs the pass:
The full implementation
`CMakeLists.txt` — the three-source module:

cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.15)
project(MiniShield CXX)

# LLVM 23 headers require C++20
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 20)
set(CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD_REQUIRED ON)
set(CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS ON)

# Find LLVM
set(LLVM_LINK_LLVM_DYLIB ON)
find_package(LLVM REQUIRED CONFIG)
message(STATUS "Found llvm ${LLVM_PACKAGE_VERSION} at ${LLVM_DIR}")
# NOTE: the installed (conda) LLVM does not provide LLVM.cmake / AddLLVM.cmake,
# so add_llvm_library is unavailable. Plain CMake + the imported target that
# LLVMConfig.cmake defines is the correct consumer pattern.
add_library(MiniShield MODULE
    lib/Plugin.cpp
    lib/FlatteningPass.cpp
    lib/StatsPass.cpp
)

separate_arguments(MS_LLVM_DEFS NATIVE_COMMAND ${LLVM_DEFINITIONS})
target_compile_definitions(MiniShield PRIVATE ${MS_LLVM_DEFS})
target_include_directories(MiniShield PRIVATE
      ${LLVM_INCLUDE_DIRS}
      ${CMAKE_CURRENT_SOURCE_DIR}/include)

# Imported target `LLVM` = libLLVM-23.so (dylib, created by LLVMConfig.cmake
# because LLVM_LINK_LLVM_DYLIB is yes for this build). Every LLVM symbol in
# the plugin resolves from the same library that opt itself loads.
target_link_libraries(MiniShield PRIVATE LLVM)

set_target_properties(MiniShield PROPERTIES LIBRARY_OUTPUT_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_BINARY_DIR})
`lib/Plugin.cpp` — both names registered:
After changing the sources or registration, rebuild and run the new name on a fixture:

cmake --build build

opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-stats),verify' \
  -disable-output tests/ir/phi.ll

Observed error: "unknown function pass 'minishield-stats'" meant the loaded plugin did not register that name. Defining a class alone does not register it. Also check that the plugin was rebuilt after adding the registration.

Observed error: "no member named 'StatsPass' in namespace 'minishield'" came from including FlatteningPass.h twice instead of including StatsPass.h. The compiler needs the declaration in this translation unit. CMake's source list supplies the implementation at link time; it does not replace includes.
Study-session walkthrough — diagnose runtime registration separately from compile-time visibility

Distinguish “unknown function pass minishield-stats” from “no member named StatsPass in namespace minishield.” The first concerns a loaded pipeline registration; the second concerns C++ declaration visibility while compiling Plugin.cpp. Including FlatteningPass.h twice cannot supply the missing StatsPass declaration.
Before writing, answer: Why can adding StatsPass.cpp to CMake still leave Plugin.cpp unable to name the class?

The include supplies a declaration while Plugin.cpp is compiled. Listing StatsPass.cpp as a target source supplies the compiled method definition later at link time. Parser registration teaches the loaded plugin a user-facing name. These are three separate connections; none substitutes for the others. A build failure may leave the previous .so on disk, so an old library can still load while lacking the new registration.
Task: Small writing step: Check the include, target source list, and callback branch, then rebuild successfully before rerunning opt.

Checkpoint: Classify the failure by stage: compiler visibility, linker definition, loader, or parser. Do not read an unknown-pass error from a stale .so as evidence that your newly edited callback was actually tested.

items: Compiler visibility: “no member named 'StatsPass' in namespace 'minishield'” means `Plugin.cpp`'s translation unit lacks the declaration. The fix is `#include "minishield/StatsPass.h"` in that file; the CMake list is irrelevant here.

Linker definition: an undefined-reference error at link time means the `.cpp` that defines the missing symbol is not in `add_library`'s source list. The fix is adding it to the target — the source list decides what is compiled and linked into the plugin.
Loader: `opt` fails to load the `.so` (wrong path, or a failed build left no usable file at `build/libMiniShield.so`). This is a `dlopen`-time problem that happens before any pass name is parsed.
Parser: “unknown function pass 'minishield-stats'” means the loaded plugin's parsing callback did not recognize the name — it is not registered, or the pipeline string is misspelled.

The stale-`.so` warning: a failed build leaves the previous `libMiniShield.so` on disk, and it loads successfully. An unknown-pass error seen through that old file does not test your newly edited callback at all, because the new callback was never compiled into it. Rebuild successfully first, then rerun `opt` — only then does the error, or its absence, say anything about the new registration.

lessons.title: Classify with a switch
lessons.originalTitle: Add instruction classifications in small increments
lessons.summary: Use LLVM opcodes to count branches, PHIs, calls, and terminators. Watch for LLVM version differences and accidental fallthrough.
lessons.takeaway: Conditional and unconditional branches have distinct LLVM 23 opcodes.

blocks.text: Now count the instruction kinds. First exercise: count conditional and unconditional branches separately. Then add switches, PHIs, returns, calls, invokes, and indirect branches. Initialize all counters before the loops and print them after traversal.
The `StatsPass.cpp` from lesson 9 already has the traversal and the total-instruction counter. Start from that, with a `switch` to classify each instruction:
Step 1 — Classify with a `switch` on the opcode

We first discussed `isa<T>(I)`, from `llvm/Support/Casting.h`, to ask whether an instruction has a particular LLVM type. The learner preferred `switch/case`. Use `switch (I.getOpcode())` with these opcode names in this installed LLVM 23 version:

llvm::Instruction::CondBr     \u2014 conditional branch
llvm::Instruction::UncondBr   \u2014 unconditional branch
llvm::Instruction::Switch    \u2014 multiway branch
llvm::Instruction::PHI       \u2014 SSA merge
llvm::Instruction::Ret       \u2014 return
llvm::Instruction::Call      \u2014 call instruction
llvm::Instruction::Invoke    \u2014 call with normal/unwind destinations
llvm::Instruction::IndirectBr \u2014 indirect branch
Step 2 — Count, `break`, and keep the total

Initialize one counter per kind before the loops, increment the matching counter inside each case, and end each case with `break`. The `default` case can do nothing. Increment `total_inst` before the `switch` so instructions such as `add` and `icmp` remain part of the total even without their own counters.
The full implementation

Observed correction: an earlier teaching example used Instruction::Br, which does not exist here. This version has separate CondBr and UncondBr opcodes. Consult llvm/IR/Instruction.def to inspect the installed names.

Observed bug: a missing break after a branch case would also increment the switch counter through fallthrough. Compilation success alone would not detect that counting mistake; the fixture expectations would.
Observed omission: switches was counted but initially absent from the printed report. Every requested metric must also appear in the output.

These are static instruction counts. One recursive call instruction can execute many times, but its static call count is still one. Count `Call` and `Invoke` separately. Branch instructions are not the same as successor edges. Loop counting is deferred to task 1.3 rather than reporting a false zero.

blocks.title: The `Call` counter also counts intrinsic calls

blocks.text: An intrinsic such as `llvm.sqrt.f64` is invoked with a `call` instruction, so its opcode is still `Call`. The `Call` counter therefore counts intrinsic calls alongside ordinary function calls — it means **all** call instructions, not just calls to user-defined functions. What an intrinsic is, and why the class chain `Instruction` → `CallBase` → `CallInst` → `IntrinsicInst` still leaves the opcode as `Call`, is in the LLVM concepts reference (lesson 19).
Study-session walkthrough — switch classification still needs the installed opcode names

A C++ switch is a suitable way to classify instruction opcodes, but use names from the installed LLVM version. LLVM 23 here has CondBr and UncondBr rather than Instruction::Br. Also check case fallthrough and ensure every counted field appears in the report.
Before writing, answer: How can a switch compile yet report a wrong count?

This is a classification fragment inside the instruction traversal. A case chooses a C++ counter update; it does not change the target branch. Without break, execution can fall through into another classification, such as also counting a branch as a switch. Names from another LLVM release may fail at compilation rather than runtime.
Task: Small writing step: Implement the two branch cases first using Instruction.def from this installation, then add the remaining opcodes and their report fields.

Checkpoint: On phi.ll expect one conditional and two unconditional branches. Its conditional contributes two CFG edges but only one branch instruction. Confirm every requested counter is printed and that a switch fixture alone increments the switch count.

items: On `tests/ir/phi.ll` expect one conditional branch and two unconditional branches: `entry` holds `br i1 %condition, label %left, label %right` (opcode `CondBr`), and `left` and `right` each hold `br label %join` (opcode `UncondBr`) — three `br` instructions total, in this installation's LLVM 23 spelling (there is no `Instruction::Br`; `llvm/IR/Instruction.def` lists the authoritative names).

The conditional branch contributes two CFG edges — `entry -> left` and `entry -> right` — because `llvm::successors(&BB)` yields both possible destinations, but it is still only one branch instruction. Instructions and edges are different measures: `phi.ll` has three branch instructions but four outgoing edges in total, which is why branch instructions are not the same as successor edges.

Confirm that every requested counter is printed — including the zeros (the observed omission was that `switches` was counted but initially absent from the printed report) — and that the switch classification works in isolation: the switch fixture (`tests/ir/switch.ll`, function `select_case`) contains a `switch` and no `br`, so its report must increment only the switch counter (one switch, three returns, zero branches), which also catches a missing-`break` fallthrough that would leak a branch count into the switch counter.

blocks.text: LLVM program before and after this checkpoint
Classifying opcodes adds C++ counters to the pass, not instructions to the target function.
The program is unchanged at this checkpoint. The report changes as classifications are implemented, but the IR remains identical.
Reading this LLVM program from zero

Do not read every displayed block as one straight-line script. A call supplies the function inputs and starts its first block. Within the selected block, follow the written instructions until a terminator chooses another block or returns to the caller. A label names a block; it does not execute an operation by itself.

rows: `define` starts a function body. `@merge` is the module-level function name; `i32` immediately before it is the return type. Parentheses contain typed inputs supplied by the caller; braces contain its blocks.

i1 means one bit: 0 is false and 1 is true for a condition; i32 means a 32-bit integer bit pattern; signed interpretation comes from operations such as slt or sdiv, not from a separate signed i32 type.

The left side names the result of this instruction. Each SSA result has one static defining instruction; input arguments are values supplied at function entry. A name is a handle for a value, not a mutable source variable or a guaranteed CPU register.

The colon defines a block label; the label operand names a jump destination. `%` is also used for local result/argument names, so use the type/context to distinguish a value from a block target. `@` instead identifies a module-level symbol.

Everything after a semicolon on that line is a comment for the reader. The printer lists incoming blocks after preds; it is not an instruction, an execution order, or a separate edge definition. Branch/switch operands actually define the edges.

blocks.text: Every instruction used in this pair

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. `br i1 %C, label %A, label %B` goes to A for true and B for false; their order matters. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Define one value by the edge just used to enter this block. Each `[ VALUE, %PREDECESSOR ]` pairs an incoming value with its source block; it is not an array access. The PHI’s i32 type applies to every incoming value, so a literal inside a bracket does not repeat the type. PHIs go at the start of a block. On a loop’s first entry choose its entry value, and on a back edge choose its carried value. Multiple PHIs select incoming values together, rather than sequentially overwriting each other.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

blocks.text: Walk one concrete execution

Call merge with condition = true: take left and obtain 10; with false, take right and obtain 20. In a PHI listing join chooses the incoming constant using the predecessor edge. In a demoted listing only the executed path stores its constant, and join reads that value.

blocks.title: Read the complete before-and-after LLVM modules

blocks.text: Before — phi original

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  br i1 %condition, label %left, label %right

left:                                             ; preds = %entry
  br label %join

right:                                            ; preds = %entry
  br label %join

join:                                             ; preds = %right, %left
  %value = phi i32 [ 10, %left ], [ 20, %right ]
  ret i32 %value
}

This listing is a complete LLVM module defining the example function, not a fragment with omitted blocks. It has no main driver unless one is explicitly included; opt can parse and verify it, while execution requires a caller. Names, alignments, and printer annotations may differ in your own output. Follow the values and edges: Both the conditional and unconditional branches retain their original destinations.

To prevent counting the next case through fallthrough
To invalidate LLVM’s cached analyses

lessons.title: Make the counts earn trust
lessons.originalTitle: Cross-check the supplied fixtures
lessons.summary: Use small fixtures with hand-counted expectations. Distinguish static instruction counts from runtime execution frequency.
lessons.takeaway: An expected table is an independent check.

blocks.text: Task: compare each report against the IR and the expected table in README.

Task 1.2's pass now reports instruction counts. This lesson makes those numbers earn trust: cross-check every report against the IR and the hand-counted expectations, instead of assuming the pass is right because it compiles.
The template — a runner for every fixture

for file in tests/ir/*.ll; do
    # run the pass and verifier on "$file"
done
Start with a loop that visits every `.ll` file. It has no comparison logic yet — it only runs the pass.
Step 1 — Read the expected counts

if-else.ll / choose:
  3 blocks; 1 conditional branch; 2 returns.

loop.ll / count_to:
  4 blocks; 1 conditional branch; 2 unconditional branches; 1 PHI; 1 return.

switch.ll / select_case:
  4 blocks; 1 switch; 3 returns.

recursion.ll / factorial:
  3 blocks; 1 conditional branch; 1 call; 2 returns.

phi.ll / merge:
  4 blocks; 1 conditional branch; 2 unconditional branches; 1 PHI; 1 return.

instruction-kinds.ll adds an invoke, an indirect branch, declarations that should not produce reports, and an optnone function that should produce one. minishield-input.ll remains the simplest load-and-run smoke fixture.
Step 2 — Run the pass and verifier on each file
Start with a shell loop to run every .ll file:
The full implementation

for file in tests/ir/*.ll; do
  echo "=== $file ==="
  opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
    -passes='function(minishield-stats),verify' \
    -disable-output "$file" || break
done

Quote "$file" so each path is passed as one argument. This loop runs the pass and verifier; it does not automatically compare the reported numeric counts against expected values. That is a separate testing responsibility.

blocks.title: Inspect function statistics (task 1.2)

blocks.text: **Status:** the statistics pass is the next implementation task. The current plugin only registers `minishield-flatten`; the fixtures below are ready for you to use while writing the pass and its test scripts.
Implement it in these steps:

items: Declare a function pass in `include/minishield/StatsPass.h` and implement `run()` in `lib/StatsPass.cpp`. Use `RequiredPassInfoMixin<StatsPass>` so inspection also runs on functions marked `optnone`.
Visit each `BasicBlock` in the function, then each `Instruction` in the block. The function pass manager already handles visiting functions.

Use `isa<T>(I)` to classify instructions. LLVM 23 provides `CondBrInst`, `UncondBrInst`, `SwitchInst`, `PHINode`, `ReturnInst`, `CallInst`, `InvokeInst`, and `IndirectBrInst`. Include `llvm/IR/Instructions.h` and `llvm/Support/Casting.h`.
Print one report per function definition to `llvm::errs()`. Skip declarations. Do not change IR; return `PreservedAnalyses::all()`.
Add `lib/StatsPass.cpp` to the existing CMake target and register `minishield-stats` in `Plugin.cpp` using the function pipeline callback.

blocks.text: After implementing and rebuilding, run:

opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-stats),verify' \
  -disable-output tests/ir/phi.ll
Suggested output format (the counts are the expected result):
[MiniShield stats] function=merge blocks=4 branches=3 cond_br=1 uncond_br=2 switches=0 phis=1 returns=1 calls=0 invokes=0 indirectbr=0 loops=deferred

`branches` counts `br` instructions, split into conditional and unconditional forms. `switch` and `indirectbr` are counted separately. `calls` counts `call` instructions, including recursive and indirect calls, while `invokes` counts `invoke` instructions separately. These are static instruction counts, not runtime execution counts. Loop counting is deferred to CFG analysis in task 1.3; print `loops=deferred` until then.
The fixtures in `tests/ir/` have these hand-counted expectations. Total `branches` is conditional plus unconditional `br`; it excludes `switch` and `indirectbr`.
`instruction-kinds.ll` also contains declarations that should not produce reports. Its `without_optimization` function has `optnone` and should still produce a report.

As a manual cross-check, open `phi.ll`: `entry` has one conditional branch; `left` and `right` each have one unconditional branch; `join` has one PHI and one return. That gives four blocks and three branch instructions.
You can validate any fixture independently of the plugin:
opt -passes=verify -disable-output tests/ir/phi.ll
Once the stats pass is implemented, confirm that inspection leaves the IR unchanged by comparing canonical output with and without the pass:

opt -passes=verify -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-before.ll
opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-stats),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-after.ll
diff -u build/phi-before.ll build/phi-after.ll
An empty diff is expected. Apply the same count and unchanged-IR checks to all fixtures when you write the test scripts. See task 1.2 in [the plan](PLAN.md) for the milestone's exit criteria.
Study-session walkthrough — write an expectation before trusting a report
Use small fixtures and hand-written expected counts as an independent oracle. A readable output table helps comparison, but its appearance does not establish that the numbers are correct.
Before writing, answer: What independent fact lets me decide whether the pass’s output is correct?

phi.ll, hand-counted:
blocks 4; instructions 5
conditional branches 1; unconditional branches 2
PHIs 1; returns 1; switches 0; calls 0

These are static properties of the fixture, not values computed by a second copy of the same counting algorithm. Read labels for blocks and actual instruction lines for instructions; comments and blank lines count as neither. Include fixtures where a field is zero as well as ones where it is nonzero, so a counter that always prints zero cannot appear correct.
Task: Small writing step: Write the expected row for one fixture before running the plugin. Compare every reported field, including zero fields that a compact table might omit.

Checkpoint: A matching table is evidence for these fixture expectations, not a behavior-preservation test. Keep expected counts separate from measured runtime frequency, and add an assertion/failure status when turning the readable report into a real test.

items: The expectations are hand counts — for example `phi.ll`/`merge`: four blocks, one conditional and two unconditional branches, one PHI, one return; `loop.ll`/`count_to`: four blocks, one conditional branch, two unconditional branches, one PHI, one return — computed by reading labels and instruction lines, not by a second copy of the counting algorithm. A report matching that table is evidence the pass *counts* correctly on known fixtures; it is not a behavior-preservation test, which asks whether a transformed program still computes the same results (a property `verify` also does not check).

Expected counts are static — what is written in the IR, fixed in place with the fixture — while measured runtime frequency is dynamic, how often an instruction executes, which depends on the input. Keeping them separate is what makes the expectation knowable by hand before the run, and including fixtures where a field is zero as well as fixtures where it is nonzero is what stops a counter that always prints zero from appearing correct.

The shell loop runs `opt` per file but does not automatically compare the reported numeric counts against expected values — that is a separate testing responsibility. Turning the readable report into a real test means the runner compares each reported field against the hand-counted row and reports an assertion/failure status (a nonzero exit) on mismatch, instead of merely printing a table.

Call count_to with limit = 2. The initial counter is 0; the signed-less-than test is true for 0 and 1, so the body increments it to 1 and then 2. At 2 the test is false and exit returns 2. A PHI selects initial 0 on entry and the previous body’s next value on a back edge; after demotion the loop-variable slot carries those same values.

blocks.text: Before — loop original

define i32 @count_to(i32 %limit) {
entry:
  br label %header

header:                                           ; preds = %body, %entry
  %i = phi i32 [ 0, %entry ], [ %next, %body ]
  %continue = icmp slt i32 %i, %limit
  br i1 %continue, label %body, label %exit

body:                                             ; preds = %header
  %next = add i32 %i, 1
  br label %header

exit:                                             ; preds = %header
  ret i32 %i
}

Because compiling and running is not proof the counts are correct

lessons.title: Give the tests a readable voice
lessons.originalTitle: Turn test_all.sh output into a readable table
lessons.summary: Capture stderr and turn the reports into a useful table. Keep a clear distinction between displaying results and asserting correctness.
lessons.takeaway: A nice table still needs expected values.

blocks.text: Task: keep the loop, but capture each opt invocation's diagnostic output:
A wall of `[MiniShield]` lines is hard to read. Turn the runner into a table that captures each `opt` invocation's report and prints it cleanly. The template is the capture structure you start from:

if output=$(opt ... 2>&1); then
    # Parse and print its report lines.
else
    # Show the file and diagnostic, then exit with failure.
fi
Step 1 — Capture stderr and guard the exit status
llvm::errs() writes to stderr, so 2>&1 redirects stderr into captured stdout. The if checks opt's exit status. A verifier failure must remain a failure, not become a plausible empty table row.
Step 2 — Print the header and parse each report line
Print the table header once before the loop using printf. The first column can use %-24s to left-align names in a minimum width of 24 characters.

For the current report format, awk -F ', ' separates fields at comma-space. Only process lines beginning with "[MiniShield] function: ". Strip that prefix from the first field to get the function name.

Fields 2 and 3 contain blocks and total instructions. Start at field 4 for the nonzero instruction highlights. Split each remaining field at ": ", and append key=value only when the numeric value is greater than zero.
The full implementation
Example table content:

Function                 | Nonzero instruction counts
choose                   | returns=2; conditional branches=1
select_case              | returns=3; switches=1

This parser depends on the report's field layout. If you rearrange the C++ report, review the parser too. Successor debug lines are filtered out because they do not match the report prefix. The table displays actual measurements; it still needs comparisons if it is to assert expected counts automatically.
Observed error: Bash reported "unexpected end of file" because the final loop-closing word was written as don instead of done. Bash reached the file's end while still expecting the loop to close.
Check syntax without executing, then run:

bash -n test_all.sh
bash test_all.sh
The syntax check is silent on success. It does not validate awk logic or whether the counts are correct.
Study-session walkthrough — a readable test runner is still a program with syntax

Treat a directory test runner as another program whose syntax and failure handling need checks. For example, don instead of done leaves a for-loop unclosed and can make Bash report “unexpected end of file,” even though the mistake is earlier.
Before writing, answer: Why does Bash point at the end of the file instead of the misspelled closing word?

for input in tests/ir/*.ll; do
    # Run opt for "$input", check its status, then format its report.
    :
done
bash -n test_all.sh

This is a loop sketch, not a replacement for your complete runner. : is a no-op placeholder. The parser tracks opened constructs such as do/if and their closing done/fi. It may only discover at end-of-file that a required closer never arrived. Separately, statistics use stderr, so command capture must deliberately include diagnostics and preserve a failure status instead of printing a successful-looking row.
Task: Small writing step: Correct the closing word and run bash -n before executing the local script. Keep test_all.sh local unless you separately choose to track it.

Checkpoint: Check a successful input and an intentionally failing command. A nice table must not hide nonzero opt status, and running all files does not assert their expected counts unless the runner actually compares them.

items: `llvm::errs()` writes to stderr, so the runner captures diagnostics with `output=$(opt ... 2>&1)` and the `if` checks `opt`'s exit status: on success it parses and prints the report lines; on failure it must show the file and the diagnostic and then exit with failure. A verifier failure must remain a failure, not become a plausible empty table row — and you can only prove that path works by exercising it with an intentionally failing command, alongside a successful input.

The table (built by `awk -F ', '` over the `[MiniShield] function: ` lines, printing `key=value` only for nonzero fields) displays measured values. Running all files under `tests/ir/*.ll` still does not assert their expected counts, because nothing compares the printed fields to the hand-counted expectations — without that comparison and a failure status, the runner exits 0 even when every count is wrong.

quiz.q: Why redirect stderr with 2>&1 when capturing the pass report?
choices: To silence the verifier on failure
Because opt only prints to stderr when a plugin is loaded
Because the report goes to llvm::errs() (stderr), so it must be merged into the captured output
quiz.why: llvm::errs() writes to stderr, so 2>&1 folds stderr into the captured stdout. The if still checks opt's exit status, so a verifier failure stays a failure, not an empty table row.

lessons.title: Prove inspection changes nothing
lessons.originalTitle: Check that inspection preserves the IR
lessons.summary: Compare canonical IR with and without the statistics pass. Understand why preserving analyses is a promise about cached data.
lessons.takeaway: Read-only passes should leave an empty diff.

blocks.text: Task: produce canonical LLVM output with and without the stats pass:
A read-only pass must leave the IR byte-for-byte identical. Prove it by emitting canonical IR with and without the statistics pass and diffing the two. Start from the plain verifier path:
The template — the before path

opt -passes=verify \
  -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-before.ll
Step 1 — Emit the after path and compare
Run the same input through the loaded plugin (the statistics pass plus the verifier), write it to a second file, and diff the two canonical outputs.
The full implementation

opt -passes=verify \
  -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-before.ll

opt -load-pass-plugin="$PWD/build/libMiniShield.so" \
  -passes='function(minishield-stats),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-after.ll

diff -u build/phi-before.ll build/phi-after.ll
An empty diff is expected and was reported by the learner. Both paths use LLVM's printer so formatting differences between the handwritten source and printed IR do not confuse this comparison.

PreservedAnalyses::all() is appropriate for this read-only pass. When the future flattening pass restructures the CFG, generally return PreservedAnalyses::none() unless particular analyses are explicitly maintained. PreservedAnalyses reports cache validity; it does not run the verifier or prove semantic equivalence.
Study-session walkthrough — prove that reading did not secretly edit the program
Compare the statistics pass with an LLVM-printed baseline to check its read-only contract. A message saying that the pass only inspected input is weaker evidence than unchanged canonical output.
Before writing, answer: Why compare two canonical LLVM outputs rather than diff a handwritten source file directly against generated IR?

opt -S tests/ir/phi.ll -o build/phi-baseline.ll

Recursion cycles between function calls, not blocks within a function. Print loops and back edges inside the one-line statistics summary if the table formatter should include them. Extra CFG diagnostic lines are filtered out by the table runner.
