items: The manager computes the analysis and owns its result, so `getResult<llvm::LoopAnalysis>(F)` hands back a reference to a cached object: binding `const auto &` lets the pass read `loopCount` without copying the loop structure into its own frame, and the result stays alive until the manager invalidates it — which the pass’s `PreservedAnalyses` return governs.

`dominates(D, B)` asks whether D dominates B, so the dominator comes first. The back-edge test needs “does the destination dominate the source”, which is why the loop writes `DT.dominates(successor, &BB)` — destination first, as the deep dive states. Swapped, the call would ask whether the source dominates the destination: the forward-edge relation, false on the loop’s own back edge (in `loop.ll`, `header` dominates `body`, not the other way round), so the test would find no back edges at all.

A back edge is an edge into a header; a natural loop is the set of blocks flowing around it. One loop can be entered by several back edges — any structure with two paths that both return to the header contributes two back edges to a single loop — so the back-edge count counts edges while `LI.getLoopsInPreorder()` counts loops (nested loops included; iterating `LI` directly visits only the top level). The two agree only when every loop has exactly one back edge, as in `loop.ll` (1 and 1); in a graph with multiple entries, cycles that are not natural loops exist in neither count.

blocks.title: Why `info.block = &BB` but `push_back(successor)` needs no `&`

blocks.text: In the basic analysis you do two different things with blocks: you **walk** them and you **store** their addresses. The walk uses a reference (`const llvm::BasicBlock &BB`), while the stored member `info.block` is a pointer (`const llvm::BasicBlock *`). Assigning the block to a pointer is a type mismatch, so store the block's address: `info.block = &BB;` — here `&` is the address-of operator, not a reference declaration. The successor loop is the mirror image: `llvm::successors(&BB)` already yields block pointers, so `successor` is a pointer and you store it as-is with `push_back(successor)`; writing `push_back(&successor)` would store a `BasicBlock **`, one level too deep. The full reference-versus-pointer treatment is in the C++ concepts reference (lesson 18).
Study-session walkthrough — fill one record completely, then append it

Build one BlockInfo per visited block, fill its fields, and append it to the returned result. Start with blocks and edges, then extend the same analysis with terminators, dominator back edges, and loop information.
Before writing, answer: Which object should info.block identify, and when should this iteration’s record be added to the result?

This is the basic run() body fragment. {} initializes each record; &BB obtains the current function-owned block’s address. Append after filling the fields so the result receives this iteration’s data. Copying a record/vector copies its pointer values, not the blocks. Request standard dominator/loop analyses only after their manager registration is in place.

Task: Small writing step: Start with block and successor records, check the diamond, then fill predecessors and final opcodes. Add reachable dominator back-edge/LoopInfo queries as the documented extension.

Checkpoint: Expect four records and four edges for phi.ll. On a loop, keep loop count separate from back-edge count: several latch edges can belong to one natural loop. The analysis itself must leave LLVM IR unchanged.

items: For `phi.ll`, `Result.blocks` should contain four `BlockInfo` records — one per basic block (`entry`, `left`, `right`, `join`) — and the recorded successor edges should total four: `entry -> left`, `entry -> right`, `left -> join`, `right -> join`, with the conditional branch contributing two. That matches the hand-drawn diamond: three branch instructions, four outgoing edges.

Keep the two counts separate: a natural loop is defined by its back edge (an edge `A -> B` where `B` dominates `A`), but several latch/back edges can belong to one natural loop, so `result.loopCount` (from `LI.getLoopsInPreorder().size()`) and the `backEdges` vector answer different questions. In `loop.ll` both are 1 (`body -> header` is the only back edge), while `phi.ll` and `recursion.ll` have 0 of each — recursion cycles between function calls, not blocks within a function.

The analysis itself leaves the IR unchanged: `run()` only records addresses, successors, predecessors, and terminator opcodes into the `Result` it returns — no instruction, block, or PHI is inserted into the module. So a canonical before/after comparison stays empty, and the printed records come from the cached analysis rather than a fresh traversal of the target.

blocks.text: LLVM program before and after this checkpoint
BlockInfo records borrow pointers to the blocks shown here. Building those records does not replace any block.
The program is unchanged at this checkpoint. Collecting predecessor/successor data leaves the entire module unchanged. Predecessor print order is not a semantic difference.
Reading this LLVM program from zero

Do not read every displayed block as one straight-line script. A call supplies the function inputs and starts its first block. Within the selected block, follow the written instructions until a terminator chooses another block or returns to the caller. A label names a block; it does not execute an operation by itself.

rows: `define` starts a function body. `@merge` is the module-level function name; `i32` immediately before it is the return type. Parentheses contain typed inputs supplied by the caller; braces contain its blocks.

i1 means one bit: 0 is false and 1 is true for a condition; i32 means a 32-bit integer bit pattern; signed interpretation comes from operations such as slt or sdiv, not from a separate signed i32 type.

The left side names the result of this instruction. Each SSA result has one static defining instruction; input arguments are values supplied at function entry. A name is a handle for a value, not a mutable source variable or a guaranteed CPU register.

The colon defines a block label; the label operand names a jump destination. `%` is also used for local result/argument names, so use the type/context to distinguish a value from a block target. `@` instead identifies a module-level symbol.

Everything after a semicolon on that line is a comment for the reader. The printer lists incoming blocks after preds; it is not an instruction, an execution order, or a separate edge definition. Branch/switch operands actually define the edges.

blocks.text: Every instruction used in this pair

rows: Meaning and operand order in these listings

`br label %B` always transfers control to block B. `br i1 %C, label %A, label %B` goes to A for true and B for false; their order matters. A branch is the block’s final instruction and produces no result. It does not execute both destinations.

Define one value by the edge just used to enter this block. Each `[ VALUE, %PREDECESSOR ]` pairs an incoming value with its source block; it is not an array access. The PHI’s i32 type applies to every incoming value, so a literal inside a bracket does not repeat the type. PHIs go at the start of a block. On a loop’s first entry choose its entry value, and on a back edge choose its carried value. Multiple PHIs select incoming values together, rather than sequentially overwriting each other.

End this function invocation and return the typed operand to its caller. `ret i32 %v` returns the integer value, while `ret ptr ...` returns a pointer. A return does not proceed to the next printed block or automatically go back to dispatch.

blocks.text: Walk one concrete execution

Call merge with condition = true: take left and obtain 10; with false, take right and obtain 20. In a PHI listing join chooses the incoming constant using the predecessor edge. In a demoted listing only the executed path stores its constant, and join reads that value.

blocks.title: Read the complete before-and-after LLVM modules

blocks.text: Before — phi original

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  br i1 %condition, label %left, label %right

left:                                             ; preds = %entry
  br label %join

right:                                            ; preds = %entry
  br label %join

join:                                             ; preds = %right, %left
  %value = phi i32 [ 10, %left ], [ 20, %right ]
  ret i32 %value
}

This listing is a complete LLVM module defining the example function, not a fragment with omitted blocks. It has no main driver unless one is explicitly included; opt can parse and verify it, while execution requires a caller. Names, alignments, and printer annotations may differ in your own output. This listing was generated and verified with the isolated LLVM 23.1.5 teaching references, not copied from an assumed completed learner implementation.
Follow the values and edges: Compare actual branch operands rather than the order of a diagnostic list.

quiz.q: What should CFGAnalyzer::run() record for each block before returning?
choices: A flattened, transformed copy of the function
The cached analysis for every function in the module
The block address, its successors, and its predecessors
quiz.why: The basic analysis reads the function without changing it: record each block's address, successors, and predecessors into a BlockInfo, append it to the result, and return. Registration and loop extensions come later.

lessons.title: The eligibility decision
lessons.originalTitle: The eligibility decision
lessons.summary: Wire the eligibility guard into the flattening stub: reject unsupported functions without changing them, isolate each rejection in its own fixture, and prove the rejected IR stays byte-for-byte identical.
lessons.takeaway: Reject before transforming; unchanged canonical IR is the contract.

blocks.text: MiniShield's product is a control-flow-flattening pass: it rewrites a function's branching into a single dispatcher. It can only run on functions it fully understands, so the first job is a guard — an eligibility policy that accepts a function only if every block, terminator, and call is supported, and rejects everything else without changing it. This is the one decision Volume 1 ends on; the flattening rewrite itself is Volume 2.
The guard returns a decision, not an edit

`FunctionEligibility::check(F)` is a plain helper: it inspects the function and returns a small result, an `eligible` flag and a `reason` string. It does not modify the function and does not need analysis-manager registration. Rejecting before any transformation is essential: a negative decision must leave the function intact, and a positive one only permits the later stages to proceed; it does not itself transform the graph.

struct Eligibility { bool eligible; std::string reason; };
Eligibility check(const llvm::Function &F);
Wire the decision into the flattening stub

In `lib/FlatteningPass.cpp`, include `minishield/FunctionEligibility.h`. After the existing declaration check, request the decision and act on it: on rejection, print the function name and reason, then immediately return `PreservedAnalyses::all()` (no edits occurred, so the cache promise holds); on acceptance, print an eligible diagnostic. The stub still changes nothing.
What the policy rejects

The guard conservatively rejects, in order: declarations (no body to flatten), presplit coroutine functions, personality routines, coroutine intrinsic calls, address-taken blocks, EH pads, and unsupported terminators. The supported terminators in this LLVM 23 API are `CondBr`, `UncondBr`, `Switch`, `Ret`, and `Unreachable`. What an EH pad, a personality routine, and a coroutine intrinsic actually are is in the LLVM concepts reference (lesson 19).
One unsupported feature per negative fixture

A function rejected for the wrong reason can hide a broken later check. So each negative fixture isolates exactly one unsupported feature: `tests/ir/coroutine.ll` targets the coroutine-intrinsic rule, and `tests/ir/address_taken.ll` targets the address-taken-block rule. An earlier unrelated rejection must not be the only reason a fixture passes.
The rejection contract: unchanged, not just valid

A rejected function must stay byte-for-byte identical in canonical form, with no partial edits. Validity alone (`verify`) is not the contract: a module can be valid yet changed. The check is a canonical before/after comparison: print the rejected function's IR with and without the pass and require the two to match.

opt -load-pass-plugin=build/libMiniShield.so \
  -passes='function(minishield-flatten),verify' \
  -S tests/ir/coroutine.ll -o build/after.ll

diff -u build/before.ll build/after.ll   # must be empty

Explain why the guard runs before any transformation, why `PreservedAnalyses::all()` is correct on the rejected path, and why an empty canonical diff, not a successful `verify`, is what proves a rejected function was left untouched.

items: The guard runs first because the flattening pass may only rewrite functions it fully understands: `FunctionEligibility::check(F)` inspects the function and returns `{eligible, reason}`, rejecting conservatively — declarations, presplit coroutine functions, personality routines, coroutine intrinsic calls, address-taken blocks, EH pads, and unsupported terminators (the supported set is `CondBr`, `UncondBr`, `Switch`, `Ret`, `Unreachable`). A negative decision must leave the function intact, and a positive one only permits the later stages to proceed, so in `lib/FlatteningPass.cpp` the decision is requested after the declaration check and the rejection path prints the reason and returns before any transformation code runs.

`PreservedAnalyses::all()` is correct on the rejected path because nothing was edited: the rejection only prints the function name and reason to `llvm::errs()`, so the promise that every cached analysis remains valid is true — the same reasoning that makes `all()` correct for the read-only `StatsPass`. (A real flattening rewrite, by contrast, generally returns `none()` unless it explicitly maintains particular analyses.)

An empty canonical diff, not a successful `verify`, proves the function was left untouched because `verify` proves only validity — that the IR obeys structural rules — and a module can be valid yet changed: a well-formed wrong transformation passes `verify` too. The rejection contract is byte-for-byte identity in canonical form: print the rejected function's IR with and without the pass (for example `tests/ir/coroutine.ll`) through LLVM's printer and require `diff -u build/before.ll build/after.ll` to be empty. Only that check rules out partial edits.

quiz.q: In the flattening stub, why reject before doing any transformation?
choices: So unsupported functions stay untouched and only eligible input is transformed
Because transformations are expensive and rejection is cheap
Because opt will not load a plugin that transforms first
quiz.why: Call FunctionEligibility::check(F) after the declaration check; if ineligible, print the reason and return PreservedAnalyses::all() (no change). Only after every check passes does the pass proceed.

lessons.title: LLVM’s in-memory object model
lessons.originalTitle: LLVM’s in-memory object model
lessons.summary: See how a module, function, block, instruction, value, and type fit together in LLVM’s C++ API.
lessons.takeaway: Follow the ownership tree and distinguish an IR label, a C++ object, and a value.

blocks.text: A pass does not edit a printed .ll file as text. It walks LLVM's in-memory C++ objects. Knowing which object contains which other object tells you where to start, what a loop gives you, and which parent owns an instruction you may erase.
The object tree for one module

rows: Shared, uniqued types and constants plus IR-wide support data
Get it from F.getContext() when creating types, constants, or blocks.
A whole IR unit: functions, globals, declarations, and module metadata
opt loads a .ll file into a Module before the pass pipeline runs.
A function definition or declaration, with its arguments and basic blocks
Function passes receive a Function; declarations have no body to flatten.
An ordered list of instructions with one entry and a final terminator
The flattener assigns state IDs to blocks and rewrites their terminators.
One operation in a basic block; result-producing instructions are also Values
The pass scans instructions for PHIs, calls, allocations, and values crossing block boundaries.
The common interface for typed operands such as arguments, constants, globals, and instruction results
IRBuilder returns Values that later instructions consume; Values also have uses.
The description of a value's shape, such as i32, ptr, or void
The eligibility guard checks result types; the state slot is i32 storage.

blocks.text: The containment chain is Module → Function → BasicBlock → Instruction. It is a useful starting point, but not every object is stored in that chain: arguments belong to a Function, constants are shared/uniqued through an LLVMContext, and types describe values rather than being executable objects.
Walk the objects in the same order

Each range supplies a reference to an existing object: the Module yields Functions, a Function yields BasicBlocks, and a BasicBlock yields Instructions. The loops do not copy the IR objects. The nested traversal mirrors the parent structure, which is why a Function pass naturally starts at F and visits its blocks and instructions.

blocks.title: Read one LLVM function as C++ objects

rows: A Function object and module-level symbol.
A Function object, module-level symbol, and GlobalValue; functions can also be Values when used as call operands.
An Argument object; arguments are Values.
A BasicBlock object. In C++, BasicBlock derives from Value, but its IR label is a control-flow destination, not an ordinary integer or pointer datum.
An Instruction object. Because add produces an i32 result, it is also a Value used by ret.
A typed integer constant Value; it is not an Instruction and executes no separate step.
A Type object describing the width/shape of the values; it is not a value itself.

blocks.text: The LLVM printer's punctuation is not a one-to-one map to C++ classes. @ names a module-level symbol; % names local values and block labels, disambiguated by syntax and position. A Value's type describes its operand/result shape, and its use-list records where it is consumed. Parent containers own their child IR nodes, so erasing an Instruction invalidates that instruction pointer; a pass collects pointers before mutation and does not use an erased PHINode afterward.

Ownership and use are different relationships. A User (such as an Instruction) contains operands; each operand is represented by a Use that points to a Value. For example, ret uses %sum. The block owns the ret instruction, while the Use links ret to the value defined by add. This use-def chain lets a transformation ask where a value is consumed without confusing that relation with which parent owns each instruction.
Ownership, identity, and pointers

A BasicBlock pointer is an address of the block object owned by its Function; it is not a copy of the block and not its printed name. The string entry is a label for humans and IR references, while pointer identity is what DenseMap uses to key state IDs. C++ references such as BasicBlock &BB are aliases for objects supplied by a range; APIs that expect BasicBlock* need &BB to receive the object's address.

This distinction matters during transformations. A vector<BasicBlock*> can store addresses of existing blocks, but it does not own them. A vector<Instruction*> can be a worklist, but after an instruction is erased its pointer is invalid. The pass must understand the parent object and the lifetime of each child it records.

Task: For the function in the deep dive, name the Function, BasicBlock, Argument, Instruction, Constant, Type, and Value objects. Then trace which C++ range supplies each loop variable in inspectModule.

Checkpoint: Why is a BasicBlock* suitable as a state-map key while the printed label entry is only a display name? Why must a collected Instruction* be discarded after that instruction is erased? How does a Use differ from ownership?

items: The BasicBlock* identifies the actual object owned by the Function, independent of its optional printed name. A label is useful for reading output but is not the block's C++ identity.
The parent owns its instructions. Erasing an instruction destroys that object, so any pointer to it becomes invalid. A worklist must not dereference or reuse it after erasure.
A Use records an operand link from a User (for example, ret) to a Value (for example, %sum). The parent BasicBlock owns the instruction; the def-use link describes how its result is consumed.

lessons.title: LLVM types and values
lessons.originalTitle: LLVM types and values
lessons.summary: Understand the i1, i32, void, ptr, and aggregate types that determine what MiniShield can transform.
lessons.takeaway: Types describe values; an address, a loaded value, and an instruction result are different things.

blocks.text: Every argument, constant, and instruction result has an LLVM Type. Types tell LLVM how to interpret an operand and which operations are legal. For a transformation, matching types is part of preserving meaning: state IDs must fit the state slot, load/store types must agree with addresses, and branch conditions must be i1.
Types the MiniShield prototype handles

rows: A store and a return from a void function produce no SSA result; skip void instructions when collecting ordinary values.
A one-bit integer value, conventionally false/true in conditions
A conditional br tests i1; CreateSelect also takes an i1 condition.
The dispatcher state slot stores i32 IDs. The guard accepts scalar instruction result types, including i32.
An opaque pointer value: an address, without a pointee type in the spelling
alloca produces a ptr; load/store spell out the accessed type separately.
Aggregate shapes, such as a struct or array
Aggregate values such as structs are outside the prototype’s scalar-value preparation path.
The parameter and return types that form a callable signature
A call's result type and a function's return type affect the support guard.

blocks.text: LLVM integer types are not signed or unsigned by themselves. i32 is 32 bits; signedness comes from an operation or predicate such as icmp slt versus icmp ult. The same bit pattern can be interpreted according to the operation using it.
A type is not a value

The type i32 describes the shape; the constant 7 is an i32 value. A C++ llvm::Type* declares a C++ pointer to a Type object; LLVM’s printed ptr is instead an IR type for an address value in the program.

llvm::IRBuilder<> B(block);
llvm::Type *i32Type = B.getInt32Ty();       // type description
llvm::ConstantInt *stateID = B.getInt32(7); // i32 constant value
llvm::AllocaInst *slot =
    B.CreateAlloca(i32Type, nullptr, "ms.state"); // instruction/value
B.CreateStore(stateID, slot);                // void-returning instruction

getInt32Ty() supplies a type. getInt32(7) supplies a constant value of that type. CreateAlloca inserts an instruction whose result is an LLVM value of pointer type: it names an address in the program. CreateStore inserts a side-effecting instruction but returns void in C++; there is no stored result to feed into a later instruction.
Read types in a small memory example
This complete function uses a condition, an integer argument, a stack slot, and a selected result. Reading each type first makes the data flow easier to follow:

blocks.title: Complete LLVM module: values, types, and memory

blocks.text:
define i32 @choose_value(i1 %condition, i32 %input) {
entry:
  %slot = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 %input, ptr %slot, align 4
  %loaded = load i32, ptr %slot, align 4
  %chosen = select i1 %condition, i32 %loaded, i32 0
  ret i32 %chosen
}

rows: Reserves stack storage for one i32 and produces its address, whose opaque pointer type is ptr.
Writes an i32 value through a ptr address. store returns no SSA value.
Reads an i32 through that address. The accessed type is written on load because ptr does not encode a pointee type.
Selects one of two i32 values using an i1 condition. Both candidate values are already available; select does not create control-flow edges or execute only one arm.
Returns an i32 value from a function whose declared return type is i32.

blocks.text: In the C++ API, I.getType() asks for an instruction's result type. A void-returning instruction has the void type even though it still exists as an Instruction. An AllocaInst is also an Instruction and a Value, but its result is a pointer to storage. These distinctions explain why the ordinary cross-block worklist skips void instructions and the allocation instruction itself.
Task: For each line in the module, name the instruction's result type if it has a result. For the alloca, load, and store, separately identify the address and the value read or written.
Checkpoint: Why is the type of %slot ptr even though it reserves i32 storage? Why does store have no %name on its left, while load does?

items: Opaque ptr represents an address and does not encode its pointee type. alloca i32 reserves storage for an i32; load i32 and store i32 state the accessed value type explicitly.
load produces the value read from memory, so it defines an SSA result. store changes memory and produces no SSA result, so it has no left-hand name and the C++ CreateStore method returns void.

lessons.title: LLVM control flow
lessons.originalTitle: LLVM control flow
lessons.summary: Read basic blocks, terminators, CFG edges, PHIs, and the state transitions that flattening must preserve.
lessons.takeaway: Terminators create the graph edges; state updates must preserve the destination each original edge selected.

blocks.text: LLVM does not represent an if/else or loop as nested syntax. It represents possible execution paths as a control-flow graph (CFG): basic blocks are nodes, and terminators at block ends define edges. The flattener's job is to change these edges while keeping the same computation and return values.
Basic blocks and terminators

A BasicBlock is a straight-line sequence: execution enters at its first instruction and proceeds in order until its final terminator transfers control or returns. A terminator must be last. A branch chooses successor blocks; ret exits the function; unreachable asserts that this point cannot execute in a defined program.

rows: The simplest edge to replace with a state store and dispatcher branch.
Chooses one of two successors using an i1 condition.
One branch instruction creates two CFG edges, and the builder must select the corresponding next state.
Chooses one case destination or its default.
The dispatcher uses a switch to turn each state ID into a block destination.
Returns a value and ends this invocation; no successor.
Returns remain terminal and should not loop back to the dispatcher.
No successor; reaching it is undefined behavior.
A dispatcher default can use it only when the state is truly impossible under the pass's invariant.

blocks.text: A conditional branch gives the graph its edges

blocks.title: Complete LLVM module: a diamond with a PHI

blocks.text: This lesson observes the module without editing it. The listing is therefore shown once; the CFG and concrete paths below are facts read from these exact instructions.

define i32 @merge(i1 %condition) {
entry:
  br i1 %condition, label %left, label %right

left:
  br label %join

right:
  br label %join

join:
  %value = phi i32 [ 10, %left ], [ 20, %right ]
  ret i32 %value
}

rows: How it controls or carries execution
The entry terminator tests the i1 value: true transfers to left, false to right. It creates two possible edges, not two executions at once.
Each arm unconditionally transfers to the shared join block.
At block entry, PHI chooses the incoming value paired with the predecessor edge just taken: 10 from left or 20 from right.
Ends the call and returns the value selected by the PHI.

blocks.text: The graph is entry → left → join and entry → right → join. With condition true, execution takes left and join returns 10; with false, it takes right and returns 20. The PHI is important because it carries path-specific data across the merge. Demoting it to a stack slot replaces that edge-based value selection with a store on each arm and a load at join.
Inspect graph edges in C++

getTerminator() returns the final instruction. llvm::successors(&BB) walks the destinations encoded by that terminator; the range yields BasicBlock* values, while iterating F yields BasicBlock references. A return block has no successors. A conditional branch has two; predecessor iteration gives the reverse relation.
From ordinary CFG to dispatcher CFG

A flattened function keeps its original work blocks but changes how execution moves between them. The pass assigns a state ID to each prepared non-entry block, stores the next ID before entering the dispatcher, and lets the dispatch switch select a block. Correctness depends on updating the state on every transition: the switch must route to exactly the block the original terminator would have selected. Entry setup runs once, and ret blocks still return rather than dispatch again.

items: Original conditional branch: test the condition and select the true or false destination's state ID.
Original switch: select the matching case destination's state ID, or the default destination's ID.
Original unconditional branch: store its sole successor's ID.
Original return: keep the return terminator; it has no next state.

blocks.text: Task: Draw the diamond's four edges before reading the PHI. Then predict how the chosen predecessor determines the returned value, and explain how the state ID must encode the same choice after flattening.
Checkpoint: Why does one conditional br create two graph edges? Why must the flattener set the state before branching to the dispatcher?

items: The branch has two label destinations, one selected for true and one for false, so the CFG records both possible outgoing edges from entry.

The dispatcher reads the state to choose the next block. If the pass branches to it before writing the correct successor's ID, it may route to a stale or uninitialized state and no longer follow the original branch choice.

lessons.title: Create instructions with IRBuilder
lessons.originalTitle: Create instructions with IRBuilder
lessons.summary: Understand the IRBuilder model and build a short typed instruction sequence that replaces a placeholder return.
lessons.takeaway: Choose where instructions go, create a value, use it, and explicitly remove obsolete instructions.

blocks.text: LLVM IRBuilder is the API this book uses to create and place LLVM IR instructions. A pass often needs more than a description of a change: it must create typed values, attach them to a basic block, and keep the function structurally valid. IRBuilder provides methods for constructing common instructions at a chosen insertion point. The pass still decides what the new instructions should mean and where control should go.
A simple way to think about it: position, create, use

A builder remembers an insertion point, which is the position where the next instruction will be placed. A Create... method builds an LLVM value or instruction there. If it returns a value, the next builder call can use that result as an operand. This lets a transformation build a small instruction sequence in execution order.

IRBuilder does not decide whether a transformation is correct and does not erase old instructions for you. It also does not promise that every Create... call inserts an instruction: when operands are constants, LLVM may fold the operation into a constant value.
Example: replace a return with x + 1
Assume the function has one i32 argument and currently returns a placeholder constant. This helper inserts an add and a new return before the old terminator, then erases the old return:

The builder is positioned before the existing return. CreateAdd inserts %sum and returns a Value* that CreateRet can use. CreateRet inserts the new terminator before the old one; eraseFromParent then removes the placeholder return. A later lesson focuses on choosing insertion points safely.

rows: Construct a builder that inserts before the existing return.
Create the typed i32 constant 1. A constant is an operand, not an instruction.
Insert an i32 add. Its result is an LLVM Value* and can feed another instruction.
Insert a return terminator that returns the computed value.
Remove the old return instruction from its parent basic block. IRBuilder does not do this automatically.

blocks.title: LLVM IR before and after this builder step

blocks.text: Before: the function returns a placeholder value.
After: the new add defines %sum, and ret returns that value.

define starts a function definition; @add_one is its module-level name. The function accepts an i32 argument named %x and returns i32. i32 is a 32-bit integer type. entry: names a basic block. In the after module, add combines %x and the constant 1 and defines the local SSA value %sum. ret i32 %sum ends this function call and returns that value to its caller. The type on add makes the literal 1 an i32 operand. The builder's constant helper supplies that typed constant; it does not print as a separate instruction.
Task: Read the helper in order. Mark the insertion point, the instruction-creating calls, the returned Value*, and the operation that removes the old terminator.
Checkpoint: Why does CreateAdd return something that CreateRet can use, while getInt32(1) does not appear as its own instruction?

items: CreateAdd inserts an add instruction and returns its resulting LLVM value as a Value*. CreateRet takes that value as its return operand.
getInt32(1) creates an i32 constant, not an operation to execute. The constant is printed inline as an operand of add, so there is no separate constant instruction.

lessons.title: Build a dispatcher with IRBuilder
lessons.originalTitle: Build a dispatcher with IRBuilder
lessons.summary: Use IRBuilder to load the current state and create a switch that maps state IDs to basic blocks.
lessons.takeaway: Create the selector, terminate the dispatcher with one switch, then attach each case to that switch.

blocks.text: A dispatcher block, built one instruction at a time

Suppose the pass has already created a dispatcher block, a default invalid block, an i32 state slot, and a list of blocks with state IDs 0, 1, and so on. This helper builds the dispatch block. It loads the current state and creates a switch whose cases map IDs to destination blocks:

This complete helper assumes its arguments are valid: the slot points to i32 storage, each state block belongs to the same function, and IDs are assigned in the vector's order. It builds one block; another part of the pass must initialize the slot and branch to the dispatcher.
What each builder call contributes

rows: Selects the end of the empty dispatcher block as the insertion point.
Gets the i32 type from the builder's LLVM context; it describes a type, not the number 32 or an i32 value.
Reads the current i32 value from the memory address held by stateSlot. The pointer is the address; the explicit i32 argument says what type to load.
Ends the block with a terminator. It compares the value with case constants, branches to the matching block, or takes the default destination.
Adds one typed integer case and its destination to the switch already created.
Makes an i32 constant used as a switch case; constants are values, not executable instructions.

blocks.title: LLVM IR before and after constructing the dispatcher block

blocks.text: The caller has the state slot and case blocks. Before this construction step, the function has no dispatcher block:

define i32 @dispatch_demo(i32 %state) {
entry:
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 %state, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %left

left:
  ret i32 10

right:
  ret i32 20

ms.invalid:
  unreachable
}
The caller creates ms.dispatch, then the helper inserts a load and switch with two cases. The complete module after that construction step is:

define i32 @dispatch_demo(i32 %state) {
entry:
  %ms.state = alloca i32, align 4
  store i32 %state, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  br label %left

left:
  ret i32 10

right:
  ret i32 20

ms.invalid:
  unreachable

ms.dispatch:
  %ms.current = load i32, ptr %ms.state, align 4
  switch i32 %ms.current, label %ms.invalid [
    i32 0, label %left
    i32 1, label %right
  ]
}
Read the instructions and syntax

rows: Defines a function named @dispatch_demo. It accepts one i32 argument and returns an i32.
Reserves stack storage for an i32 and produces a pointer to that address. align 4 is an alignment promise in bytes.
Writes the argument value to the address in %ms.state. A store has no SSA result.
Transfers control to left. A label is a block destination, not an instruction or data value.
Ends this function call and returns the selected integer to its caller.
Marks a point that must not execute in a defined program; it is not a fallback return.
Reads one i32 from the address and defines the SSA result %ms.current.
Chooses one destination by comparing %ms.current with the typed cases; unmatched values take the default invalid block.

blocks.text: The function signature define i32 @dispatch_demo(i32 %state) defines a function named with @; it accepts one i32 input and returns an i32. Here i32 is a 32-bit integer type. %state is the argument value; %ms.state and %ms.current are local SSA names, while left, right, and ms.dispatch name basic blocks. The % prefix is shared, so syntax and position tell you whether a name refers to a value or a block. The %state argument is stored to the address produced by alloca i32. store writes a value to that address. br label %left transfers control to left, where ret i32 10 ends the call and returns 10. The right block similarly returns 20. unreachable says the invalid block cannot execute in a defined program; it is not a fallback return.

In the after module, load i32, ptr %ms.state reads the saved state into the SSA value %ms.current. The pointer type ptr names the address; the following i32 tells load which value type to read. The switch compares the loaded value with typed constants 0 and 1, transfers to the corresponding case block, and sends every other value to ms.invalid. Labels are destinations, not instructions.

The switch cases add CFG edges to left and right, and the default adds an edge to ms.invalid. No edge enters ms.dispatch yet: entry still branches directly to left, so this newly constructed switch is disconnected and does not affect execution. That is an intentional intermediate stage. A later step stores a state ID and rewrites the entry edge to reach the dispatcher. Both complete modules are well-formed, but verify alone proves neither completed flattening nor behavior preservation.
Where the builder writes matters
When adding instructions to an existing entry block, inserting at its end may put an instruction after the terminator, which is invalid. Instead, construct the builder before the old terminator:

This inserts the alloca before the old terminator. An alloca i32 reserves stack storage for an i32 and returns a pointer to it; it does not itself store the current state. A later CreateStore writes an ID there. For the special entry-block setup rule used in this project, entry->getFirstInsertionPt() is another way to choose the first legal insertion point, after any PHIs.

Use a separate builder for a separate block, or call SetInsertPoint when you intentionally move one builder. A builder remembers its insertion point; it does not infer the desired block from the operands.
Study-session walkthrough — construct and inspect a dispatcher

Start with the intended graph on paper: a state value is loaded, the switch chooses one block, and its default edge goes to the invalid block. Then match each edge in that plan to one API call: CreateLoad makes the selector, CreateSwitch creates the terminator and default edge, and addCase attaches each state-to-block mapping. Check that the chosen insertion point is before any existing terminator and that no instruction is appended after the switch.

Task: In StateMachineBuilder, use one builder for the dispatcher. Add the load and switch, then attach a case for every (state ID, block) pair. Keep slot initialization and entry rewrites as separate steps.

Checkpoint: Explain which call inserts an instruction, which calls only provide a type or constant, and why addCase does not append a second terminator. Inspect the resulting block with opt and run the verifier.

items: CreateLoad inserts the load and returns its LoadInst*; CreateSwitch inserts the switch terminator and returns its SwitchInst*. getInt32Ty() returns a type and getInt32(id) returns a constant, so neither is an instruction. addCase mutates the already-created switch's case list; the block still has one terminator.

The insertion point determines where CreateLoad and CreateSwitch go. A builder for a new empty dispatcher starts at its end; for an existing block, use an insertion point before its terminator. The switch must remain last. The verifier checks structural validity, while inspecting the cases confirms the intended state mapping.

blocks.text: Check your understanding
If B.getInt32(2) returns a value, why does it not appear as an instruction in the printed block?
Answer: It is a constant operand, not a computation to execute. The switch uses the constant as a case label; LLVM prints the value inline in the switch.

lessons.title: C++ concepts
lessons.originalTitle: C++ concepts behind the LLVM calls
lessons.summary: Reference cards for the C++ behind the LLVM calls: references versus pointers, the two jobs of &, and how a range-based loop variable gets its type.
lessons.takeaway: References bind existing objects; pointers hold addresses. & declares in a type, addresses in an expression.

blocks.text: Reference cards for the C++ the Volume 1 lessons rely on: references versus pointers, the two jobs of `&`, and how a range-based loop variable is typed. Look these up when a construct matters; each entry states the idea, shows it in this project's code, and links the language reference.
Reference versus pointer

A **reference** is another name for an existing object; a **pointer** is a variable whose value is an object's address. A reference must always name a real object, so it can never be null or reseated; a pointer can start empty and be assigned. In the CFG analysis you walk a function's blocks by reference and store their addresses as pointers.

Use `BB.getName()` through the reference and `block->getName()` through the pointer. `BlockInfo` stores pointers, not references, because a result is plain data that can start empty and be assigned; a reference would not fit a `std::vector` or a default-initialized member.
`&` in a type versus `&` in an expression
The same glyph does two different jobs depending on where it sits. In a type, `&` declares a reference; in an expression, `&` is the address-of operator.

const llvm::BasicBlock &BB     in a TYPE:       & declares a reference
&BB                            in an EXPRESSION: & is address-of, yields BasicBlock *

In `info.block = &BB;`, the `&` asks for the address of the block that `BB` names, producing a `BasicBlock *`, which is exactly what the pointer member holds. Storing a reference where a pointer is expected (`info.block = BB;`) is a type mismatch.
Storing an address, versus storing a pointer as-is
Take the address to fill a pointer member, but do not re-take the address of a value that is already a pointer.

info.block = &BB;                        // BB is a reference; &BB obtains its address
info.successors.push_back(successor);    // successor is already a BasicBlock *; store as-is
info.successors.push_back(&successor);   // wrong: a BasicBlock **, one level too deep
`auto` and loop-variable copying
`auto` deduces a type but does not preserve the reference the iterator supplies. A plain `auto` variable copies the element; when the element is noncopyable, that copy fails to compile.

This is why `for (auto bb : F)` fails: `llvm::BasicBlock` is noncopyable. But `auto` is not always wrong. For a range whose elements are already pointers, a plain `auto` copies only the pointer value, not the pointed-to block.
Follow the range's element type

There is no rule that every traversal uses `&` or every traversal uses `*`. The loop variable's type follows what the range supplies: references for existing objects you inspect without copying, and pointer variables when the elements already hold addresses.

for (const llvm::BasicBlock &BB : F)                     // F yields block references
    for (const llvm::BasicBlock *s : llvm::successors(&BB))  // successors() yields block pointers

See the C++ reference for [references](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/reference.html), the [address-of operator](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/operator_other.html), [auto](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/auto.html), and the [range-based for loop](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/expressions.html).

quiz.q: What does &BB mean in info.block = &BB?
choices: Copy the BasicBlock
Declare a new reference
Obtain the address of the block that BB refers to
quiz.why: In this expression, & is address-of. In a declaration such as BasicBlock &BB, it declares a reference.

lessons.title: LLVM concepts
lessons.originalTitle: LLVM concepts the guard relies on
lessons.summary: Reference cards for the LLVM constructs the eligibility decision mentions: exception-handling pads, personality routines, and intrinsics.
lessons.takeaway: Pads receive the unwind; a personality routine enables them; an intrinsic call keeps opcode Call.

blocks.text: Reference cards for the LLVM IR constructs the eligibility decision mentions: exception-handling pads, personality routines, and intrinsics. Each entry states what the construct is, how it appears in IR, and the guard rule that involves it.
Exception-handling pad (EH pad)

The word **pad** comes from **landing pad**: a place where control arrives when an exception interrupts normal flow. An `invoke` names two destinations, `to label %normal` and `unwind label %exception`. The unwind destination begins with a landing pad, after any PHIs.

%result = invoke i32 @callee()
    to label %normal
    unwind label %exception

exception:
  %ex = landingpad { ptr, i32 } cleanup
  resume { ptr, i32 } %ex

LLVM recognizes `landingpad`, `catchpad`, `cleanuppad`, and `catchswitch` as EH-pad instructions. `cleanup` marks participation in cleanup handling; it does not run destructors by itself. `resume` continues unwinding. The guard rejects any function that contains an EH pad, because rewriting EH edges as ordinary dispatcher edges would require semantics the prototype does not implement.
Personality routine

A personality routine defines a function's language-specific exception-handling behavior. Two queries inspect different levels: `F.hasPersonalityFn()` asks whether the function specifies one (function-level), while `BB.isEHPad()` asks whether a block's first non-PHI instruction is an EH pad (block-level). A block containing `invoke` is not itself a pad; the pad is the unwind destination.

Valid EH-pad instructions require a personality routine, so rejecting every personality function up front already rejects functions with valid pads. The later block-level check is therefore redundant for those inputs; it states the unsupported block kind explicitly.
Intrinsic

An **intrinsic** is a special function whose meaning LLVM itself defines. Its name has the reserved `llvm.` prefix and it is declared without a body. It is commonly written as a `call` rather than a new opcode.

In the C++ API the class chain is `Instruction` to `CallBase` to `CallInst` to `IntrinsicInst`: every intrinsic call is a call and an instruction, but most instructions and calls are not intrinsic. The statistics pass's `Call` counter still counts intrinsic calls, because the invoking instruction's opcode is `Call`; recognizing an intrinsic does not change that opcode.

The guard conservatively rejects coroutine intrinsics: after `llvm::dyn_cast<llvm::IntrinsicInst>(&I)`, a callee name starting with `llvm.coro.` is rejected. See [LLVM's exception-handling docs](https://llvm.org/docs/ExceptionHandling.html), the [intrinsic reference](https://llvm.org/docs/LangRef.html#intrinsic-functions), and [coroutines](https://llvm.org/docs/Coroutines.html).

quiz.q: Why does the successor loop use a pointer while the block loop uses a reference?
choices: Pointers are faster than references in any loop
The range supplies the element type: F gives blocks by reference, successors() gives block pointers
The & in &BB inside successors() declares a reference
quiz.why: Follow the element type, not the punctuation. Iterating F yields references to existing blocks; llvm::successors(&BB) yields block pointers, so the variable is a pointer. &BB there is address-of, not a declaration.

lessons.title: Look up a term
lessons.originalTitle: Glossary. Terms used in the README and Volume 1
lessons.summary: The working glossary for the README and Volume 1: every term used in the guide, defined in one to three sentences with a pointer to the lesson where it appears.
lessons.takeaway: If a term is new, the glossary is the fastest detour.

blocks.text: Alphabetical, one-to-three-sentence definitions of the terms that appear in the README or in this guide, for readers who met them before they were explained. "See lesson N" points to where the term is used; the lesson's deep dives go further than the entry here. Entries marked (Background) are covered by the Background lesson (lesson 0) that opens this book.

rows: The machine-level contract between compiled code and its libraries: calling convention, object layout, and which shared-library symbols exist. Switching the LLVM release changes the headers and ABI, which is why the plugin must be built against exactly the LLVM release that `opt` runs (see lesson 2, "which installation" row).

A basic block whose address is used as a value in the IR (produced by `blockaddress`). Such a block is a value a program can compute with, not just a control-flow destination, so the flattening policy rejects it (see lesson 24).

A CMake command that creates a library target — a named node in the build graph carrying sources, compile/link rules, and requirements. The type keyword (`STATIC` / `SHARED` / `MODULE`) decides the artifact (see lesson 2, "What does add_library do?").
A small text-processing language for line-by-line field work. `awk -F ', '` splits each input line into fields at the first comma-plus-space separator (see lesson 13).

An edge `A -> B` in a CFG where `B` **dominates** `A` (every path from the function entry to `A` passes through `B`). Every natural loop has at least one; in `loop.ll` the edge `body -> header` is the only back edge (see lesson 17).
A straight-line run of instructions with one entry point, no jumps inside, and a terminator at the end. Basic blocks are the nodes of a CFG (Background).
An LLVM operation that yields the address of a named basic block as a value: `ret ptr blockaddress(@f, %target)`. It is what makes a block "address-taken" (see lesson 24).
LLVM IR serialized to a compact binary format (`.bc` files); `opt`'s default output. `-S` requests text IR instead (see lesson 7).
The file CMake + the Ninja generator write into `build/`: the complete list of compile and link rules. "Ninja could not find build.ninja" means configuration did not complete (see lesson 3).

CMake has no array type; a "list" is a string whose elements are separated by `;`. A space-joined string is one element, which is why `LLVM_DEFINITIONS` must pass through `separate_arguments` before use (see lesson 2, "What does separate_arguments do?").
The C and C++ compilers of the LLVM project. The conda environment exposes `clang++-23` (no plain `clang++`), so the configure command pins that path explicitly (see lessons 1, 3).

A package and environment manager (Miniforge is a common conda distribution that defaults to the conda-forge channel). The `minishield` environment is a self-contained directory with one consistent toolchain — its own compiler, LLVM 23.1.5, and build tools — so the project does not depend on the host machine's C++ setup (see lesson 1).

A named directory prefix holding one consistent set of packages. Creating it installs packages into that prefix; activating it only changes the current shell so the environment's tools are found first (see lesson 1, checkpoint).
The directory an environment is installed into (for example `~/miniforge3/envs/minishield`). "Separate prefix" means packages do not mix with the system's or other environments' (see lesson 1).

An environment variable set by `conda activate`, holding the path to the active environment. Recipes like `$CONDA_PREFIX/bin/clang++-23` and `export LIBRARY_PATH=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib` are how you point CMake and the linker at that environment's tools (see lessons 1, 3).

A function that can be suspended and resumed. In LLVM IR it is expressed through `llvm.coro.*` intrinsics. A **presplit coroutine** is a coroutine function the front end has already split into continuation blocks, detectable with `F.isPresplitCoroutine()` (see lessons 22, 23, 25).

The header files of `libstdc++`, the C++ runtime. Conda installs the runtime (`libstdc++.so`) and its development headers as separate packages; a missing `<type_traits>` means the `libstdcxx-devel_linux-64` package is absent, not that an LLVM header is misconfigured (see lesson 1).

A declaration (`declare i32 @foo(i32)`) announces that a function exists, with no body; a definition (`define i32 @foo(i32 %x) { ... }`) provides the body. Passes only run on definitions; `F.isDeclaration()` detects the former (see lessons 9, 22).

The POSIX function that loads a shared library at run time and returns a handle to its symbols. This is the mechanism behind `-load-pass-plugin=...`: the plugin is a load-time relationship with `opt`, not a link-time one (see lesson 2).
Block B dominates block A when every path from the function entry to A passes through B. Dominance underpins the back-edge definition and the `DominatorTreeAnalysis` (see lesson 17).

A shared library. LLVM's dylib in this environment is `libLLVM-23.so` (about 188 MB); `opt` loads it, and the plugin resolves its LLVM symbols against the same copy at load time (see lesson 2, "Where does the size go?").

The first instruction of a block that receives exceptional control: `landingpad`, `catchpad`, `cleanuppad`, or `catchswitch`. The name comes from landing pad. `BB.isEHPad()` asks whether the block's first non-PHI instruction is one of these (see lesson 21).
In a C `switch`, control continuing into the next `case` because the current case has no `break`. A missing `break` after a branch case was the counting bug of lesson 11.
A small stable input file with known-by-hand expected results (here, the `.ll` files in `tests/ir/`); "fixed in place" as test setup (Background).
A C++ declaration granting another type access to private members. `friend llvm::AnalysisInfoMixin<CFGAnalyzer>;` lets the mixin reach the analysis's private `AnalysisKey` (see lesson 16).
A C++ unit-testing framework; installed in the environment now and used by the later C++ test suite (see lesson 1).

A file in LLVM's source that lists every opcode name; the authoritative spelling reference for this version (`CondBr`, `UncondBr`, `Switch`, ...). There is no `Instruction::Br` in LLVM 23 (see lesson 11).
LLVM's type-testing and type-casting helpers: `isa` answers "is this value a T?" and returns a boolean; `dyn_cast` returns a `T*` on success and `nullptr` otherwise (see lessons 11, 22).

A special function declared by LLVM itself, with names in the reserved `llvm.` namespace (for example `llvm.sqrt.f64`, `llvm.coro.noop`), whose semantics LLVM knows and which is lowered directly to target code. In IR it appears as an ordinary `call` instruction with opcode `Call` (see lesson 22).
The typed, SSA intermediate representation that compiler stages operate on; `.ll` files are text IR (Background).

An environment variable the compiler driver reads for link-time library search directories. Conda's clang does not search `$CONDA_PREFIX/lib` by default, so the export makes `libstdc++.so` findable. It is a different thing from `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (which affects runtime library loading) and from `LLVM_DIR` (which tells CMake where the LLVM CMake package lives) (see lessons 1, 3).
The LLVM linker; installed in the environment for future toolchain work (see lesson 1).
The block a thrown exception "lands" on; see EH pad (lesson 21).

LLVM's standard loop finder. A natural loop is a back edge's target (the header) plus every block that can reach the header without going through the exit. `getLoopsInPreorder()` lists nested loops in tree **preorder** (parent before children); iterating the `LoopInfo` object directly visits only the outermost loops (see lesson 17).
The smallest fixture: one function, one block, one `add`, one `ret` (see lesson 7).

The three CMake library types: `STATIC` builds an object archive (`libX.a`) whose code is copied into each consumer; `SHARED` builds a linkable shared object (`libX.so`) consumers record a `DT_NEEDED` entry for; `MODULE` builds a loadable plugin (`libX.so`) that nothing links against and that is loaded via `dlopen()` (see lesson 2).

A base class that contributes one concern — here, pass metadata such as the pass name — to a pass class. `OptionalPassInfoMixin` vs. `RequiredPassInfoMixin` decide whether the pass may be skipped (see lesson 5).
The build tool that executes `build/build.ninja`. "No work to do" means every rule's outputs are up to date; it is not a test result and not a failure (see lessons 2, 3).
LLVM's IR command-line tool: read IR, run a pipeline of passes, write IR and diagnostics (Background).

A function attribute meaning "do not optimize this function". Optional passes (like `FlatteningPass`) are skipped on `optnone` functions; required passes (like `StatsPass`) still run there (see lessons 5, 23).
The operation code of an instruction: `add`, `icmp`, `br`, `call`, `ret`, ... `Instruction::getOpcode()` returns it; the exact spellings in LLVM 23 are listed in lesson 11.
Print text IR / write the output to a file / keep the result in memory and print no IR (Background).

The colon-separated list of directories the shell searches for commands. `conda activate` puts the active environment's `bin/` at the front of it, which is what "activation" accomplishes (see lesson 1).
One program-level inspection or transformation that LLVM runs over the IR, once per object, in scheduled order (Background).

The C++ class that turns a pipeline string like `function(minishield-stats),verify` into actual pass instances and managers. A plugin registers its passes with the `PassBuilder` through the callback it returns from `llvmGetPassPluginInfo` (see lesson 6).

The `-passes=` string: an ordered list of pass invocations with nesting groups such as `function(X)` (run X once per function), `module(Y)`, or `loop(Z)`; a comma separates consecutive stages (Background).
The C++ structure a plugin's entry point returns: the plugin API version, the plugin name, the plugin version, and the callbacks that register passes with the `PassBuilder` (see lesson 6).

The function a language runtime calls while an exception unwinds, to decide how the exception is handled (in C++ it is `_Unwind_Resume`). A function that can receive exceptions carries one; `F.hasPersonalityFn()` asks whether it does (see lesson 21).

An instruction that, at the entry of a block, picks which value flows in from which predecessor: `%x = phi i32 [ 1, %left ], [ 2, %right ]`. It exists because of SSA: instead of redefining a value's name at a merge point, the merge point explicitly selects among incoming values (lesson 7; Background).

A constant from `llvm/Plugins/PassPlugin.h` identifying which plugin ABI the plugin was written against; the host checks it matches before loading. It is separate from the plugin's own version string (see lesson 6).
For block B: predecessors are the blocks with an edge into B; successors are the blocks with an edge out of B. `llvm::predecessors(&BB)` / `llvm::successors(&BB)` yield them (see lesson 15).
A tree traversal order in which a parent is listed before its children. `getLoopsInPreorder()` therefore lists an outer loop before the loops nested inside it (see lesson 17).

The value a transformation pass returns, describing which cached analyses remain valid after its changes. `::all()` says "nothing was touched" (correct for read-only passes like `StatsPass`); `::none()` says "assume every cached analysis is invalid" (the safe default for a real transformation). It reports cache validity only — it does not run the verifier or prove behavior was preserved (see lessons 4, 14).
A compiler directive meaning "include this header at most once per translation unit" (see lesson 8).
`CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`: the compiler is asked to optimize the plugin and omits debug-oriented checks (see lesson 3).

A reference (`const BasicBlock &BB`) is another name for an existing object; a pointer (`const BasicBlock p`) stores an object's address. `&BB` takes the address of the referenced object; `p` dereferences a pointer (see lessons 18, 19).

A compiled object loaded at run time and shared by every user of it. `libLLVM-23.so` and `build/libMiniShield.so` are both shared objects; the first is linked against (recorded in `DT_NEEDED`), the second is loaded via `dlopen()` by `opt` (see lesson 2).
The canonical name recorded inside a shared library, which consumers record in their `DT_NEEDED` entries so the runtime loader knows which file to load (see lesson 2).

The rule that every value in LLVM IR is defined exactly once and used only after that definition. Jumps and merges are handled by PHI nodes instead of redefining names; `verify` checks the SSA constraints (lessons 6, 8; Background).

A static count counts what is written in the IR: one `call` instruction counts as 1 no matter how many times it executes at runtime. A dynamic count would count runtime executions. Every count in MiniShield so far is static (see lesson 11).

Stream 1 (stdout) carries normal output; stream 2 (stderr) carries diagnostics — `llvm::errs()` writes there. `2>&1` merges stderr into stdout so a `$(...)` command substitution can capture both (see lesson 13).
A placeholder implementation that exists and runs but does not do the real work yet; a "diagnostic stub" is one whose only job is to print observations (Background).
A named node in CMake's build graph carrying its sources, compile/link rules, and the requirements attached by the `target_*` commands; `add_library` creates one (see lesson 2).
Human-readable LLVM IR (`.ll`); `-S` requests it. The compact default is binary IR (see lesson 7).

The last instruction of a basic block; it transfers control: `br`, `switch`, `indirectbr`, `ret`, `invoke`, or `unreachable`. The current flattening policy accepts `CondBr`, `UncondBr`, `Switch`, `Ret`, and `Unreachable` only (see lessons 11, 23).

One `.cpp` file, expanded with the headers it includes and compiled into one object file. Each translation unit needs the declarations of the classes it uses; the CMake source list decides which translation units get compiled and linked into the plugin (see lesson 4).
A terminator marking a point that cannot execute (for example after an infinite loop or a checked precondition); it transfers control nowhere. The flattening policy accepts it (see lesson 23).
An `invoke` instruction calls with two exits: `to label %normal` and `unwind label %exception`. Unwinding is the exceptional exit; it lands on an EH pad (see lesson 21).

CMake's model of who sees a target's compile/link requirements: `PRIVATE` = the target itself only, `PUBLIC` = the target and its consumers, `INTERFACE` = consumers only. MiniShield is a plugin nothing links to, so everything is `PRIVATE` (see lesson 2).
`verify` proves validity (the IR obeys LLVM's structural rules); it does not prove correctness (the transformed program behaves the same as the input) (Background).
A built-in pass that checks IR structural validity: types, SSA constraints, PHI incoming edges, return types, and related invariants. It succeeds silently on valid IR (Background; lesson 7).
